# AGENTS.md

High-level guide for the whole repository. Each area has its own `AGENTS.md` with
the rules that apply only there; the nearest one applies in addition to this file.
Read the area file before changing code in that area.

## Overview

**Korus** is an Electron desktop app for coordinating teams of coding agents with
native conversation and artifact rendering, plus a mobile companion, a hosted
telemetry collector and the public website. Stack: TypeScript throughout, Vue 3 and
Element Plus for UI, Electron Forge for packaging, Vitest for tests.

Core product surfaces: **Teams** (top-level grouping), **Agents** (named teammates
with folders, backend sessions and status), **Conversation** (native chat, tool
calls, approvals, plans, diffs) and **Artifacts** (document, plan, diff, git and file
panes beside the conversation).

## Repository Map

| Area | What it owns | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `core/` | Platform-neutral product contracts, backend protocol, state primitives. | [core](core/AGENTS.md) |
| `client/` | Desktop: `backend` (local daemon), `electron` (main, preload, packaging), `vue` (shared UI); `cli` (standalone terminal recovery and control). | [client](client/AGENTS.md) |
| `mobile/` | iOS and Android companion apps and their shared engine. | [mobile](mobile/AGENTS.md) |
| `native/` | Native helper binaries shipped with the desktop app. | [native](native/AGENTS.md) |
| `server/` | Hosted telemetry collector and private admin console. | [server](server/AGENTS.md) |
| `website/` | Landing page, privacy policy, VitePress user guide. | [website](website/AGENTS.md) |
| `videos/` | Scripted product films. | [videos](videos/AGENTS.md) |
| `docs/`, `scripts/`, `plans/` | Engineering notes, repo tooling (incl. the architecture lint), saved plans. | |

`core/`, `client/*`, `mobile/` and `server/*` are npm workspaces. `npm run dev`
launches the Electron app.

## Architecture At A Glance

`core/src/product.json` owns product branding and external identity. Keep
identifiers, package names, filenames and CSS brand-neutral; read product metadata
for visible names, paths and packaging. Authored documentation may use the name.

Areas are isolated on purpose and `npm run lint:architecture` enforces it: shared
inputs flow through `core`, and nothing imports across runtime boundaries (mobile
and the collector never import the daemon; the renderer never imports backend
protocol types). On the desktop, Electron main is the adapter, `daemon`
(`client/backend`) owns backends, providers, persistence and filesystem access, and
the renderer owns visual state. See [client/AGENTS.md](client/AGENTS.md) and
[docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).

## Mobile API Compatibility

Every endpoint and wire contract the mobile app consumes must stay strictly
backwards compatible with shipped mobile clients: shared desktop/mobile endpoints,
streamed events, serialized provider data and SDK upgrades alike. Desktop-only
endpoints have no such requirement. Never require a mobile update to keep existing
operations working; keep old request and response semantics, and introduce
incompatible behavior only through explicit opt-in negotiation or a separate version.
Changes affecting mobile need released-client regression evidence at the owning
runtime boundary before handoff, commit or push; tests of only the newest client are
not enough. See [protocol.md](docs/protocol.md#mobile-compatibility) and
[testing.md](docs/testing.md#mobile-compatibility-evidence).

## Documentation

`AGENTS.md` files stay high-level. Docs under `docs/` are reference for the current
state: ownership, invariants, gotchas and their reasons. They do not restate what
code, types, scripts or config say, do not walk through UI behavior (specify that in
tests), and carry no dates, "now/no longer/previously" narrative or decision history
(that is git history). Fix a stale doc in place. Update docs only when an
architecture, process or reusable convention changes.

- `docs/architecture.md`: process model, ownership rules, persistence, remote teams,
  worktrees, Missions, code review, work providers.
- `docs/protocol.md`: JSON-RPC conventions, synchronization, lifecycles.
- `docs/testing.md`: testing principles, Test Value Gate, fixtures, coverage, gates.

Each area file lists the docs that belong to it. Discuss a new doc with Nicolas
first; if approved, add it under `docs/` and link it from the owning area.

## Quality

Every behavior change needs coverage at the owning runtime boundary, and the
behavior test is written before the production change. For docs-only or untestable
changes, say so in the handoff. Prefer E2E and integration tests, apply the Test
Value Gate, never delete or weaken a failing test to pass the suite, and never read
source files as text in a test. Every workspace gates on exactly 85% statement
coverage; do not lower it or shrink the measured surface. All of this, with the CI
behavior, is in [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md); read it before editing code.

The gate is `npm run lint` plus `npm test`. Run focused tests while iterating and
the relevant gate before handoff.

Fixed real-time sleeps are forbidden in all Vue tests and browser test helpers
(desktop, console, mobile web and website). Use observable conditions or
controlled clocks, as described in [testing.md](docs/testing.md).

## Build

Use the Node 26 reference toolchain (`.nvmrc`, `package.json`). Keep build outputs,
generated bindings and packaged resources separate from source. Packaging and
signing are in [client/AGENTS.md](client/AGENTS.md).

**SDK.** Dev builds run the `~/src/codex-app-sdk` source (`CODEX_APP_SDK_SOURCE=1`), so
SDK changes are live: never cite publishing or the pinned version outside release prep.

## Project Skills

Repo-local skills live in `.agents/skills/`; read the matching `SKILL.md` before
editing. Use `korus-dod` before handing off, committing, pushing or calling work
done. Others: `korus-frontend-dev` (Vue, app shell, design tokens),
`korus-testing-coverage` (Vitest, fakes, coverage), `korus-live-preview` (isolated
Electron previews), `korus-desktop-update` (signed desktop update and restart),
`update-changelog` and `prepare-release` (release notes and tagging).

Never update `CHANGELOG.md` during ordinary implementation, review, handoff, commit
or push; curate it only when Nicolas invokes `update-changelog` or `prepare-release`.

## Working Agreements

- **Plans** only when Nicolas asks or plan mode is active. Review a plan with him
  before saving it under `plans/` (never `~/.Codex/plans`) as `feature-name.md`, with
  implementation strategy, test strategy and commit checkpoints. Update it each phase
  and append learnings at the end.
- **Commits** are single-line, lowercase, prefixed `feat:`, `fix:`, `test:` or
  `chore:` (`chore:` also for docs-only).
- **Before handoff or commit**: `git status --short`, review the diff, stage only
  files relevant to the task, `git diff --check`, run the relevant tests or say why
  not. Do not revert unrelated changes, and never use destructive git commands
  unless Nicolas explicitly asks.

# client

The desktop product. Follow the root [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) too; shared contracts
live in [`core/`](../core/AGENTS.md). `backend` is the local daemon (`daemon`),
`electron` is desktop main, preload and packaging, `vue` is the shared Vue UI (also
used by the mobile web views), and `cli` owns standalone terminal recovery and
control. The CLI may reuse backend modules while remaining runnable without
Electron or a running daemon. Electron Forge, TypeScript, Vue 3 with Element Plus,
Vitest.

## Process Boundaries

- Electron main is the desktop adapter: windows, preload IPC, native dialogs, app
  lifecycle, packaged resources, and the stdio client that reaches `daemon`.
- `daemon` owns backend processes, drivers, provider protocols, approvals, server
  requests, persistence, filesystem access, git, automations and agent runtime state.
- The renderer owns visual state and interactions. It never talks to a provider,
  spawns tools, reads arbitrary local files or depends on backend protocol types.
- Preload is a small, typed, explicit IPC bridge. Coordination events become
  app-owned before reaching the renderer; provider traffic stays inside an app-owned
  routing envelope.
- Backend-dependent features enter through app-owned contracts and the protocol first:
  extend a driver method or capability behind `daemon`, route Electron through
  `BackendClient`, keep renderer components free of Codex/Claude branches.
- Theme with semantic tokens and CSS variables; no hard-coded product colors.

## Providers

Codex and Claude Code run as provider drivers in `daemon`. Provider conversations
stay provider-owned: `codex-app-sdk` owns the Codex snapshot, reducer, history, turn
mutations and generic conversation UI, and Korus stores the thread reference,
transports snapshots and events, and adds coordination metadata. Fix generic Codex
behavior in the SDK; Codex product policy lives in the driver. `RendererMessage` is an
app-owned DTO where explicitly needed, not a live transcript. New providers arrive as
hosts behind `daemon`, not as a global transcript reducer. `CODEX_APP_SDK_SOURCE=1`
links `../codex-app-sdk` (`CODEX_APP_SDK_SOURCE_ROOT` for another checkout).

Optional telemetry is isolated by lint: only the local runtime composes the uploader,
provider and pricing code cannot depend on it, and its endpoint is runtime config.

## Packaging, Docs And Verify

Forge signs and notarizes macOS builds by default, which is slow and reserved for
release work; for verification use `APP_SKIP_SIGNING=1 npm run package` (or `build`).
Read: `docs/backend-architecture.md` (daemon rules, packaging, auto-update, companion
gateway and relay), `docs/codex.md` and `docs/claude.md` (provider integration),
`docs/mcp.md` and `docs/custom-tools.md` (MCP server and tools), `docs/frontend.md`
(UI, with the `korus-frontend-dev` skill), `docs/agent-provider-selection.md`,
`docs/agent-isolation.md` (unimplemented design note), `docs/codex.png` (target shell) and
`docs/research/` for dated evidence. Test with `npm test -w @workspace/backend`,
`-w @workspace/vue`, `-w @workspace/electron` or `npm run test:integration`; check UI
in the real app with `korus-live-preview`.

# core

`@workspace/core` holds the platform-neutral product contracts and state
primitives that every other area builds on: app-owned types, the backend protocol,
snapshot and reducer logic, and pure helpers shared by the desktop, the mobile
app and the hosted console. Its modules are imported by path (`@workspace/core/<module>`
maps to `src/<module>.ts`). Follow the root [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) as well.

## Rules

- **Stay platform-neutral.** No Electron, daemon, provider SDK or browser-only
  dependencies. The mobile app and the hosted console import `core` too, so a new
  import here widens what they can reach. Keep helpers pure and side-effect free.
- **App-owned contracts first.** Backend-dependent product features enter through
  the contracts and the backend protocol in `src/backend-protocol/`, then the
  daemon, then the renderer. `docs/protocol.md` has the conventions; the method
  catalog is the code.
- **Wire contracts are compatibility surfaces.** Anything the mobile app reads
  (companion protocol, projections, notifications, shared endpoints) must stay
  backwards compatible with shipped mobile clients. Extend with optional fields or
  explicit negotiation; never repurpose or remove one. See the Mobile API
  Compatibility section of the root file and `docs/testing.md`.
- **Product identity lives in `src/product.json`.** Read it for visible names,
  URLs and paths; do not hard-code the product name in identifiers, package
  names, filenames or CSS.
- **Telemetry and usage contracts are closed.** The telemetry projection, the
  collector and the private console may import only an allowlist of `core`
  modules; `npm run lint:architecture` enforces it. Add a field only with its
  consumers in view, and never put prompts, paths or other user content into a
  telemetry contract.
- **Days are decided on read.** Usage is stored with exact timestamps and the
  reader's timezone decides which day a turn belongs to (`usage-time`).

## Verify

- `npm test -w @workspace/core` and `npm run lint -w @workspace/core`; the
  statement coverage gate is 85% like every workspace.
- Contract changes need a test at the owning runtime boundary in the consumer
  (daemon, renderer, mobile), not only in `core`.

# Claude Code Integration

Korus drives Claude through the official `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`, only from
`daemon` (`client/backend/src/claude/`). The SDK launches Claude Code with its native
settings, skills, hooks and project instructions; Korus never calls the Messages API
or replaces Claude Code with a generic model loop. Read this before changing
Claude sessions, history, permissions or capabilities. Dated runtime evidence and
unsupported cases are in
[research/claude-capabilities.md](research/claude-capabilities.md); read it before
adding steering, forks, goals, turn mutations or context controls.

## Session Model

- Each live session owns one long-running SDK query; later turns use its streaming
  input rather than a new process per prompt. A persisted agent without a live query
  resumes through the SDK `resume` option. At most one idle live query is kept per
  agent: switching conversations releases the previous one, and an identity,
  instruction, MCP or permission-safety change restarts and resumes it so stale
  configuration cannot leak into later turns.
- The transport configures the Claude Code system-prompt and tool presets, user,
  project and local setting sources, the agent's folder/model/permission mode, the
  Korus MCP server and its allow rule ([mcp.md](mcp.md)), and partial streaming
  events. Prompt and developer text travels over the SDK input stream and is kept
  out of process logs. The executable is launched directly, not through a shell;
  the shared runtime resolver supplies the login-shell executable and child PATH
  because GUI-launched Electron can inherit a different environment.
  An installed CLI takes precedence over the SDK-owned native runtime packaged with
  Korus; source development can use the SDK optional dependency directly.
  `APP_CLAUDE_COMMAND` overrides resolution without falling back if it is broken.
  Detection, queries, authentication and version inspection share this policy.
  The packaged runtime updates with Korus, not through a CLI package manager.
  Query processes use the product slug as `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` when unset or
  inherited as `cli` or `sdk-*`, so upstream quota attribution identifies the app.
  Explicit custom entrypoint labels are preserved; the parent environment is unchanged.
- The Claude conversation host is the sole owner of the normalized transcript. It
  maps SDK stream messages to immutable `ClaudeConversationEvent`s, keeps one
  snapshot per agent and publishes a bounded reset plus revisioned deltas
  (`claude.conversation*` frames). `AppSnapshot` never contains Claude messages.
  Conversation refreshes republish the open live session; transcript history is read
  only when no live session exists, and an in-flight history read cannot replace a
  session started meanwhile.
- A shared semantic adapter turns tool use (Bash, Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep, web,
  Skill, MCP, and tools such as todos, tasks, subagents and worktrees)
  into app-owned titles, paths and statistics for both live and historical
  records. Read/Write/Edit/NotebookEdit also emit file activity so file links and
  Git status stay current.
- Native Agent/Task executions project into the shared subagent tree, including
  completions after the parent turn ends. Child transcript reads carry the parent
  session and child ID; sidechain messages stay out of the parent's conversation.
  Cold history rebuilds children from structured native tool results and marks
  unfinished workers interrupted when their owning query is gone.
- Tool rows reach the renderer as the same status descriptors Codex produces, so
  both providers read alike. Simple read-only shell commands (`cat`, `ls`, `rg`,
  and similar) are classified into read, list and search; anything with shell
  syntax or an unrecognized flag stays a plain run, because a wrong summary is
  worse than the literal command. Tools with no file or command shape carry a
  `scope` and `operation` in the descriptor, and the renderer owns the wording.
  A tool the adapter does not know falls back to the SDK's generic title.
- **Outcome ordering.** Explicit interruption is reported before failure, and
  failure before success. An error result or unexpected iterator end emits a failed
  outcome even after a durable task result was submitted (that result stays
  provisional). An asynchronous interrupt callback settles only its own turn and
  cannot clear a newer one on the same session. Readiness and task success are
  separate.
- Native text has no work/final phase. The shared grouping rule keeps all text
  after the last work tool visible as the answer, or all response text when there
  are no work tools. Korus status/completion tools, reasoning and continuation
  input do not move that cutoff. Explicit phases retain their provider semantics.

## Homes And Authentication

- Korus honors one process-wide `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` for SDK queries, transcript
  hydration, Resume discovery, personal skills and plan streaming; per-query
  overrides are unsupported. Startup applies the persisted home. Defaults, sharing,
  isolation and roster-reset rules are in
  [architecture.md](architecture.md#provider-homes).
- **Leave `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unset for the default `~/.claude`.** The CLI treats
  setting even that same path differently for credential lookup, so auth checks, SDK
  child processes and displayed login commands must agree; local authentication
  returns a null `configDirectory` for the default. Keyless Console profiles live
  outside `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and are not isolated credentials.
- Credentials stay Claude-owned: Korus never copies tokens or settings, and they
  never enter IPC, snapshots or renderer state. Login is `claude auth login
  --claudeai` (subscription) or `--console` (API billing) run by the user on the
  owning host, including SSH hosts, which each authenticate their own home. Login
  commands use the selected executable path, so a separate CLI install is optional
  on desktop. Expired logins are renewed by Claude Code, not Korus.
- Authentication failures emit `provider.authenticationChanged` with
  credential-free metadata; the daemon updates its observation and publishes
  immediately, leaving enablement and existing conversations intact (service errors
  and usage limits do not imply logout). Before admitting new work the daemon
  re-probes an engine last seen disconnected, so an external login makes the next
  retry succeed. This is not continuous polling.
- Subscription usage is fetched on demand by `daemon` from the CLI-internal
  `api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage` endpoint (needs `user:inference` and
  `user:profile`) using the configured home's login in place. It is not a stable
  public API: errors are bounded and reported separately from accounts without
  quotas, and API-key billing has no usage row.
- Installation is user-managed. Welcome and Settings link to Anthropic's official
  instructions and can recheck PATH on the owning host without running an installer.
  Discovery adds `~/.local/bin` for non-interactive SSH launches.
  Onboarding offers both engines independently and needs at least one authenticated.

## History And Resume

Transcripts are read from Claude Code's JSONL files at
`<home>/projects/<project-dir>/<session-id>.jsonl` (project dir is the absolute
folder with non-alphanumerics replaced by `-`; `sessions-index.json` can point to
the file), not through the CLI. Only displayable records are read: user text,
assistant text, tool use/result (same adapter as live), and structured `goal_status`
records. Queue operations, `last-prompt`, sidechains and meta command records are
ignored. Hydration also restores the latest model and effort, falling back to the
agent's last used.

Explicit mention metadata is scoped to the provider session and the native input
UUID assigned at submission. Records live under the configured home's
`prompt-content` directory, follow native forks, and are removed with the session.
Hydration uses only matching authored records; text and current catalogs cannot
create historical mention identities.

The host opens recent history using the SDK's current-chain message UUIDs. A
backward native-file read extends that slice to complete prompt boundaries and
recovers metadata the SDK omits, including prompt IDs and compaction markers.
Both paths use the same native normalizer; SDK rows are never independently
assigned turn identities. The SDK may still scan the file, so this does not make
cold reads constant-time. Empty, unavailable, or unmatched SDK history falls back
to the native reader. Isolated homes cannot use a different process-wide SDK home.

Scrolling beyond the recent slice hydrates the native archive, including history
before compaction, and prepends bounded pages through the existing driver seam.
Each page has message-count and serialized-byte budgets. The archive joins at the
original recent message identities, preserves expanded details, and excludes
later file appends owned by the live replica. Replacement, truncation, or a changed
join requires reload. Archive failures retain the recent view and allow retry;
concurrent requests share the read. The index and cursor are ephemeral and cleared
on release or session replacement. Delayed reads cannot replace another session.
Starting new provider work also hydrates a deferred archive first, restoring native
task, goal, and subagent state before continuation. This state upgrade keeps the
visible transcript window intact; historical state cannot overwrite a live query.
Compaction context remains inside its original turn; internal summary records do
not create user messages or duplicate turn identities.
Completed historical turns publish summaries with prompt and final-answer content.
An ephemeral byte-range index keeps Working content in the native file until
expansion. Selected ranges are verified against their indexed hashes; appends are
safe, while replacement or changed bytes require a reload. Unchanged files reuse
the open index and cached expansions. Exhaustive reads retain the original native
projection and authored mentions.
Working expansion sends the complete selected turn through the same conversation
replica, including segments outside the visible page. Insertion anchors preserve
source order; older paging skips already loaded rows. Details errors are retryable,
concurrent requests share one read, and results for a released or superseded
session cannot mutate its replacement. Live turns retain full detail.
Interrupted-session continuation hydrates history before starting the live turn,
so the live replica retains its older-page cursor.

Oversized message content stays on the owning host behind an agent/session-scoped
content reference. The conversation carries a preview; explicit reads retrieve the
exact message JSON in bounded base64 chunks, including duplicated native tool
fields and Unicode. Content updates invalidate superseded references. Clients
render fetched content locally and never put it back into provider snapshots.
History prepends and context updates are revisioned deltas. Reconnect snapshots
contain a bounded recent window rather than accumulated scroll-back pages; the
companion forwards older-page frames directly and rechecks authorization after
content reads.

A long conversation never travels whole: the daemon opens the most recent rows within a
byte budget (so one event stays far under the 4 MiB limit and a phone never receives a
frame it cannot take) and prepends older pages on demand. Loaded Working rows are shown as they are. Only a
part that is huge on its own (a screenshot, a file dump) is cut to a preview, and a row
that would still not fit is cut part by part, never dropped. The exact row stays readable
by content ID in bounded chunks. The desktop pane reads a cut row in the background as it
appears and shows nothing to press: a row too large to be worth reading keeps its preview,
as does a client that cannot read content, such as the phone.

**Canonical cwd gotcha:** Claude stores the resolved path (`/tmp` is
`/private/tmp` on macOS), so history and Resume discovery check both the logical
and the resolved path, dedupe session IDs, and keep reads working for removed
workspaces. Resume lists an agent folder's sessions newest first, returns opaque
`ConversationSummary` rows, and is allowed only while the agent is idle.
Folderless Quick Chats use the home directory as cwd (user skills only) and keep a
null folder reference.

## Capabilities And Policy

- Quota rejections retain their reset metadata even when the native result
  envelope says success. Session-limit error text with an explicit timezone can
  supply a reset deadline when structured metadata is absent. The daemon owns
  automatic continuation policy.
- **Scheduling:** sessions connected to Korus exclude Claude's native cron and
  wakeup tools through SDK `disallowedTools`. Recurring prompts use Korus's
  persisted automations and require an explicit user request ([mcp.md](mcp.md)).
- **Models:** local aliases `opus`, `sonnet` (default), `haiku` until a short-lived,
  non-persisting SDK query reads the live catalog on agent selection; names,
  descriptions and supported efforts come from the SDK, so the effort selector
  appears only for models that advertise it. Effort is passed on the first turn and
  updated later via the runtime settings API.
- **Speed:** models advertising native fast-mode support use the shared speed
  selector. Speed changes resume the native session in a new query, since the SDK
  requires launch-time opt-in. Managed/account restrictions remain authoritative;
  explicit fast-mode unavailability fails before prompt submission. Execution
  analytics stores the configured tier; request pricing uses reported billing evidence.
- **Permissions:** Claude's own modes (`default`, `acceptEdits`, `dontAsk`, `auto`,
  `bypassPermissions`) are exposed through a capability-driven submenu and routed
  as opaque mode IDs the driver validates against what it advertises;
  `bypassPermissions` also sets the SDK's dangerous-skip gate. Native `plan` stays
  behind the separate Plan control. These are distinct from Codex approval presets.
  Permission callbacks and `AskUserQuestion` normalize into the provider snapshot
  and project into the composer's `confirm_tool` requests using the exact
  transcript part ID; responses use the agent-targeted client-response path.
- **Plan mode** is `planMode: "prompted"`: the driver keeps the prompt unchanged and
  starts the turn with native `permissionMode: "plan"` (not the `/plan` slash
  command, which is unavailable in some SDK environments). `EnterPlanMode` and
  `system/status.permissionMode: "plan"` mark planning; the private plan-file
  `Write` streams as `turn.proposedPlanDelta` and is not rendered as a tool;
  `ExitPlanMode.input.plan` becomes `turn.proposedPlanCompleted`. The app-owned
  agent plan is the source of truth, not Claude's file. Comments keep Plan mode and
  send a follow-up; confirming clears it and sends the implementation prompt.
- **Task lists:** confirmed native Task tool results and legacy `TodoWrite` updates
  project into the existing execution-plan panel. Task IDs come from structured
  results; failed operations do not advance progress. The Claude host retains the
  session's task projection, rebuilds it from native history before paging, and
  transports the resulting plan with conversation frames. Proposed-plan review
  remains separate. Sessions opt into native todo tools for progress display.
- **Attachments:** supported images, PDFs and text/source files go as native content
  blocks; other binaries are available by trusted local path.
- **Context and compaction:** usage comes from `getContextUsage()` after init, turns
  and compaction, plus a short-lived non-persisting query when a persisted
  conversation is selected. `/compact` is Claude-owned and routed silently;
  boundaries are restored from history and reuse the common compaction lifecycle.
- **Skills:** listed from the filesystem (user skills under the configured home,
  project skills under `<folder>/.claude/skills`, project overriding global,
  symlinked directories followed, broken links skipped).
- **Goals, steering, same-folder forks, resume:** implemented. Steering is
  boundary-dependent, not an immediate interrupt; the transport owns queued input
  until the SDK replays its UUID and the work completes, and stopping a steered turn
  closes its query. Fork cutoffs come from persisted native boundaries; goal state
  comes from structured `goal_status` records, with clear distinct from completion.
- Worktree delegation uses the SDK's native session fork in the source store,
  then resumes the child query in the worker's folder with its own model,
  permissions, system appendix and MCP identity. A running source is cut at its
  last completed live native boundary; without one it starts a fresh handoff.
  The persisted session keeps its native transcript folder separately from the
  execution folder; reads, further forks and deletion use that storage reference.
  Interactive same-folder forks retain their idle-source guard.
- Rollback, edit, retry and delete-turn stay unsupported; enabling any further
  control needs evidence at the SDK and driver boundaries first.
- **Code review** defaults to a separate visible reviewer in the same workspace
  ([architecture.md](architecture.md#code-review)). Inspection turns must call
  `finish_review_round({ findingCount })` and Korus waits for the turn to end;
  native `ReportFindings` calls do not populate the ledger.

## Request pricing evidence

The SDK transport owns numeric request capture. The driver attaches the Korus
execution identity and forwards observations to the persistent usage ledger before
analytics calculates historical costs. Conversation history is not a pricing source.

- `message.id` identifies one API response across assistant blocks and partial
  events. The optional assistant `request_id` is retained as upstream correlation.
  `parent_tool_use_id` retains child correlation; the originating tool's execution
  owns late child samples even while a subsequent user turn runs.
- `message.model` is the actual model. The first live response observation
  (normally `message_start`) supplies an immutable local timestamp; the public SDK has no server request-start timestamp.
  Configured model aliases and fast settings are not served billing evidence.
- Input is disjoint: `input_tokens` excludes `cache_read_input_tokens` and
  `cache_creation_input_tokens`. Their sum supplies the pricing context measure.
  `cache_creation.ephemeral_5m_input_tokens` and `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` must sum
  to total creation. Explicit zero creation proves no writes; missing positive-write
  lifetime detail remains unknown, regardless of configured TTL.
- Assistant `output_tokens` is a message-start placeholder. Cumulative
  `message_delta.usage.output_tokens` supplies measured output; a terminal delta
  or message stop establishes finality. Assistant-only output remains unknown.
  Output already includes thinking; an unknown thinking split is retained as null
  and can be priced only if it cannot change any category's rate or adjustment.
- `usage.service_tier`, `speed`, and `inference_geo` retain actual capacity tier,
  inference mode, and region. The pricing catalog's fast tier corresponds to
  reported fast speed, separately from capacity tier. Missing speed/tier is
  explicit. Priority commitments and batch tier have no supported catalog rules
  and remain unpriced. Pricing attribution checks both the launch environment and
  the SDK-resolved user, project, local, and managed settings before consuming
  usage. Cloud/proxy routing or conflicting routing in either layer stays
  unpriced. Settings-resolution failures and unresolved policy helpers also
  leave the provider unknown without preventing the conversation from running.
- A single `message` iteration can omit `model` and uses the enclosing message's
  served model. An explicitly different model, multiple server-side `iterations`,
  or a different iteration kind retain an unsupported pricing reason. They need a
  richer pricing projection; no turn-wide context or cheaper rate is substituted.

Request samples replace earlier revisions of the same response. Result `usage`
continues to supply execution token/timing analytics and never creates request
charges. Complete main-loop coverage requires reconciliation of all four numeric
result categories against final captured requests. Missing identities, mismatched
or absent totals, interruption without final evidence, and child activity retain
unknown additional-request coverage. Measured child costs contribute, but the
public SDK lacks the final per-child totals needed to attest a complete child set.

These rules follow the public [Agent SDK usage contract](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking),
[cache token semantics](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching#tracking-cache-performance),
and [reported inference speed](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#checking-which-speed-was-used).
The fake-query workflow retains a reproducible $0.1386 example across three
responses, with a fixture context predicate at 200,000 tokens, 407,980 cache-read tokens,
50 five-minute writes, 100 one-hour writes, mixed models, and fast US inference.

## Tests

`configured-home.spec.ts` covers restart, history and resume routing, symlinked
skills, private plan streaming and real SDK deletion against temporary homes. Its
scripted queries prove Korus routing, not browser login or live-model persistence;
verify those against a real Claude Code install. Normal tests use a fake SDK query
([testing.md](testing.md)).

# mobile

The iOS and Android companion apps and the engine they share. They reach a paired
desktop through the companion relay. Follow the root [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) as
well; shared contracts live in [`core/`](../core/AGENTS.md).

## Layout

- `src/`: the shared TypeScript engine (companion transport, request ledger,
  conversation and draft state, caches). Tested with Vitest.
- `web/`: the Vue views hosted inside the native apps, built on the shared
  `@workspace/vue` UI.
- `native/`: the Noise session bundle the native shells use for the secure link.
- `ios/`: the SwiftUI app, its Swift package and tests.
- `android/`: the Kotlin app and its tests.
- `app-store/`: store artwork and listing assets.
- `scripts/`: native and browser verification runners.

## Rules

- **Strict backwards compatibility.** Every endpoint and wire contract the app
  consumes must keep working for shipped clients. This is the root Mobile API
  Compatibility rule; the evidence belongs at the owning runtime boundary and the
  handoff names the released-client baseline.
- **Mobile is isolated from the desktop runtime.** It never imports Electron, the
  daemon, desktop packages or provider SDKs (including the Claude Agent SDK); it
  consumes `core` contracts and the companion protocol only.
  `npm run lint:architecture` enforces it.
- **The desktop owns the work.** The phone shows and drives agents that run on the
  laptop. Do not add behavior that assumes the phone can run agents, hold
  provider credentials or reach a repository directly.
- **Keep the native shells thin.** Product logic, state and caching live in the
  engine so iOS and Android behave the same and can be tested in Vitest. Native
  code owns platform concerns: secure storage, notifications, dictation, layout.
- **Apple toolchain.** Run Xcode commands through
  `node mobile/scripts/ios.mjs xcode <arguments>`, including archives and exports.
  The wrapper gives Apple's system tools precedence over user-installed copies
  so distribution packaging uses compatible tools.

## Verify

- `npm test -w @workspace/mobile` and `npm run lint -w @workspace/mobile`.
- Native, scroll and release checks are separate scripts in `package.json`
  (`test:native`, `test:native:*`, `test:scroll`); run the ones for the platform
  you changed. Build or install on a device only when the task asks for it.
- Docs: `docs/backend-architecture.md` (companion gateway and relay invariants)
  and `docs/testing.md#mobile-compatibility-evidence`.

# native

Native helper binaries shipped with the desktop app. Follow the root
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) as well.

## tts-helper

`tts-helper/` is a Swift package that builds `app-tts-helper`, the local
text-to-speech helper. `npm run build:tts` (`scripts/prepare-tts-helper.mjs`)
builds it and copies the binary into the desktop app's resources (`client/electron/.tts`).
Electron main launches it for spoken announcements; the renderer never talks to it.

- **The request protocol is versioned.** `SpeakRequest` carries a version, an id,
  the text and an optional voice, and the helper validates all of it (version,
  non-empty id and text, a short text limit). Change the protocol additively and
  keep the version check honest.
- **Everything is local.** The helper uses an on-device model. Voice tensors are
  downloaded on demand and verified against pinned SHA-256 digests before use;
  never relax that check or add a network dependency.
- **Dependencies are pinned and attributed.** When `Package.resolved` or the model
  changes, update `NOTICE.md` in the same change.
- **Verify** with `swift test` in `native/tts-helper`; these tests are not part of
  `npm test`.

# server

The hosted telemetry collector and the private admin console. They are deployed
and run independently of the desktop and mobile apps. `README.md` in this folder is
the reference; read it before changing the collector, its migrations, its
deployment or its privacy behavior. Follow the root [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) as
well.

- `backend/`: the independently bundled Node collector (ingestion and read
  modes) on PostgreSQL.
- `frontend/`: the private Vue admin console.
- `deploy/`: portable Docker services.
- `scripts/` and `test/`: image packaging and the end-to-end server checks.

## Rules

- **Independent runtimes.** The collector imports only the closed shared telemetry
  contracts and its PostgreSQL client; it never imports the desktop daemon,
  providers or the companion relay, and none of those import it. The console
  imports no client code and consumes browser-safe aggregate contracts from
  `core`. `npm run lint:architecture` enforces both directions.
- **Privacy is a release gate.** The collector retains no IP addresses or report
  content, and it has no request logger. Do not add logging, headers or fields
  that could identify an installation or carry content. A local test cannot prove
  the production guarantee; say so in the handoff.
- **No DDL at runtime.** Migrations are explicit, versioned and run under an
  external role. Ingestion never creates or alters tables.
- **Secrets stay out of Git and bundles.** Database URLs and operator credentials
  are read at runtime from operator-managed files or environment; builds are
  tested for secret canaries.
- **Shared inputs are packaged explicitly.** The server uses `core` contracts and
  product metadata; keep that dependency list small and explicit so this folder
  can be extracted.

## Verify

- `npm run test -w @workspace/server-backend` (needs Docker, it starts disposable
  PostgreSQL containers) and `npm run test -w @workspace/server-frontend`.
- `npm run test:server:e2e` and `npm run test:server:infrastructure` for the
  console and deployment checks.
- Building or testing never authorizes publishing, activating an endpoint or
  deploying; those are separate approved Ship actions.

# Promotional videos

This folder contains editable, scripted Korus product films. Follow the repository-root `AGENTS.md` as well as these film-specific conventions.

## Before building a film

1. Inspect the closest existing film and its thumbnail. Reuse the series' app shell, typography, pacing, controls, and interaction language where they fit.
2. Check the current product UI and behavior for the workflow being promoted. Keep panes, actions, and shipped capabilities recognizable. Promotional motion can exaggerate a real transition; label the result as an illustration rather than a live recording.
3. Default to a 16:9, 1600×900 film. Make a 9:16 cut only when Nicolas asks for Shorts/TikTok/vertical format.

## Source and motion

- Keep editable HTML, CSS, and choreography in `videos/`; Remotion in `remotion/` owns Studio playback, audio, frame rendering, and encoding. Register films in `film-catalog.mjs` and the composition controller registry. Use the shared Remotion exporter for every film.
- Keep controllers importable without starting browser playback. Drive visual state from `createFilm(root).seek(seconds)`; the standalone browser adapter exposes `window.seekFilm` for previews. Remotion supplies the frame clock. Random-access scrubbing and parallel exported frames must tell the same story at the same timestamp.
- Preserve each film's authored CSS cascade. Load only the active composition's styles so another film cannot override them. Wait for artwork and fonts before rendering.
- Use `film-timing.mjs` to map frames to the approved narration. Preserve continuous takes, their provenance, and measured captions; a re-export must not invoke speech synthesis. Optional captions stay separate WebVTT tracks.
- Carry the viewer through the workflow with movement inside the app—typed prompts, progressing work, panels, diagrams, and objects moving into their next state. Use scene transitions sparingly; avoid a sequence of fade-outs/fade-ins or decorative wave/shift effects.
- Keep progress causal and legible. A task or defect should advance through its stages rather than jump to completion or reset visually.

### Cursor and clicks

Match the earlier films' cursor treatment (see `review-film-controller.mjs` and `delegation-film-controller.mjs`):

- Schedule only meaningful clicks as `[start, click, selector]` against the actual rendered target. Derive its center from `getBoundingClientRect()` relative to the scaled film, rather than hard-coding screen coordinates.
- Ease the cursor in from nearby, briefly scale it down on press, and show one short ripple (about 0.28 seconds) at the target. Hide cursor and ripple outside that click's interval.
- Inspect frames immediately before, during, and after each click. The pointer must land on the control that changes state; a continuously blinking ring or cursor floating over unrelated content fails this check.

## Assets and handoff

- Track editable film source in `videos/` and thumbnail artwork in `videos/assets/`. MP4s and poster frames are rebuildable outputs and stay ignored by Git. Do not add other generated artifacts to the repository.
- Keep the thumbnail consistent with the existing series: a strong, readable headline and a recognizable product visual. Do not rely on tiny fake UI copy to explain it.
- Preview the film in a browser and inspect representative frames for every stage, all scene boundaries, and each click. Export the MP4, confirm dimensions, frame rate, duration, and decoding, then inspect frames from the **rendered video** as well as the live viewer.
- Update `website/README.md` with the new viewer and export command. State what is illustrative, and hand off the editable source, tracked thumbnail, and ignored rendered MP4 separately.
- These standalone films are verified through deterministic playback, media checks, and visual inspection. Do not add brittle source-text or snapshot tests for choreography; add automated tests if reusable application behavior or a shared contract changes.

# website

The public site: the static landing page, the privacy policy and the VitePress
user guide. `README.md` in this folder has the build, preview and publishing
notes. Follow the root [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) as well.

## Rules

- **Write for users, in the present tense.** Describe what people can do and what
  they get, not how it is built. Document the current product only: no release
  planning notices, "coming in" labels, comparisons with other versions, history
  or acknowledged gaps. Version history belongs in release notes.
- **The guide and the engineering docs are separate.** The public guide is
  `docs/` here (VitePress, navigation Getting started, Providers, Workflows,
  Features, Reference, Troubleshooting). Internal notes stay in the repository's
  top-level `docs/` and are never published. Keep the sidebar in
  `docs/.vitepress/config.mts` in sync with the pages.
- **Product facts come from `core/src/product.json`.** The build expands the
  name, canonical URL and download links; do not hard-code them.
- **The privacy policy is authored in `privacy/index.html`.** Keep its contact
  links inside Cloudflare `email_off` comments. Any privacy or telemetry promise
  is published only after the release gate in the README is met, and with the
  matching Analytics guide.
- **Building does not publish.** Deployment (`deploy.sh`) is a separate approved
  Ship action.

## Verify

From the repository root: `npm run docs:check`, `npm run test:website`,
`npm run test:docs` and, for navigation changes, `npm run test:website:browser`.
Preview the built artifact (see the README) so both the landing page and the guide
render with product metadata.

# Desktop Update

Use the bundled [updater](scripts/update.py) for the local installed macOS app and
its owned stdio daemon. Remote hosts and independent daemon services use their
own deployment tools.

From the source checkout, choose one command:

```bash
python3 .agents/skills/korus-desktop-update/scripts/update.py deploy
python3 .agents/skills/korus-desktop-update/scripts/update.py restart
python3 .agents/skills/korus-desktop-update/scripts/update.py status
```

- `deploy` builds, signs, notarizes and smoke-tests the current working tree, then
  stages the replacement. Validate source changes with `korus-dod` first; a clean
  or committed tree is not required. Use `--repo` for another approved checkout.
- `restart` stages an identical copy of the installed app without rebuilding.
- `status` reads the latest transaction's startup checks and rollback outcome.

Use existing restart/deployment authorization and explain the brief mobile
reconnection and possible interruption of active tasks. Discussing the workflow
or reading status does not authorize activation.

The switch delay defaults to **30 seconds**. Once the command returns `armed`,
report activation as pending and finish the provider turn promptly. Independent
one-shot installer and recovery LaunchAgents perform the switch after the turn
ends. After reconnect, check `status`: `complete` confirms startup and pairing;
`rolled_back` means the previous app was restored; `recovery_failed` requires
operator intervention. Exercise the updated feature separately.

Credentials stay in the existing private `.env`/Keychain setup. Transactions,
logs and sensitive profile backups live under `$APP_HOME/desktop-updates` (or the
product's default home), outside Git checkouts. Keep provider history in place and
retain backups until cleanup is requested. Sanitize logs before sharing; process
diagnostics show only PID, PPID and executable names because arguments can contain
credentials. Consult `--help` for explicit path overrides.

name: korus-dod
description: Use before handoff, commit, push, or declaring Korus work ready. Verify scope, tests, typecheck/lint, documentation, and worktree hygiene with proportional evidence.
---

# Korus Definition Of Done

Gather the smallest evidence that proves the change is ready. Add broader gates
only when the change crosses a boundary.

## Inspect

```bash
git status --short
git diff --check
```

Review the diff against the latest request. Account for every changed file and
preserve unrelated user changes.

For code changes, call Korus `get-diff-stats` when available, choosing the scope
that covers the work being reviewed (for example, `branch` when the work spans
commits). Compare the changed lines of code and tests. When test changes are
disproportionately large relative to the code change (for example, one line of
code and 100 lines of tests), scrutinize whether that amount of testing is
justified by the behavior and risks. Inspect the tests for redundant scenarios,
overlapping workflows, and opportunities to consolidate without losing meaningful
regression coverage. Apply the Test Value Gate in `docs/testing.md` and make
warranted improvements within the task's scope. Use judgment rather than a fixed
ratio; don't weaken tests merely to reduce their size. If the tool is unavailable,
compare the diff directly. Exclude unrelated changes from your conclusions.

## Verify

Run every applicable row. For release-only metadata and dependency preparation,
use the release row instead of the implementation rows:

| Change | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Docs/config only | `git diff --check` |
| Scoped code | Focused workspace test and affected workspace typecheck |
| Mobile-consumed contract or producer, including SDK upgrades | Released-client request/response/event regression through the owning runtime; old behavior retained without a mobile upgrade, with new behavior negotiated or separately versioned |
| Visible frontend | Scoped-code gates plus one targeted runtime, DOM, or screenshot check |
| Imports, exports, dependencies, CSS, or shared config | Relevant lint command |
| Cross-cutting | `npm run test:ai` and affected workspace typechecks |
| Coverage-sensitive | Focused coverage; use `npm run test:coverage` only when repository-wide evidence is needed |
| Release | Local metadata checks from `prepare-release`; release CI gates ordinary tests independently of Quality coverage. Report CI as pending at dispatch, not locally validated. |

The coverage gate is exactly 85% statements in every workspace, including
Electron. Lines, branches, and functions remain reported diagnostics. Meaningful
behavioral/regression tests and owning-boundary verification remain mandatory;
a coverage percentage alone is not proof of correctness.

Use package-local Vitest for focused tests:

```bash
npm run test -w <affected-workspace> -- <focused-file-or-pattern>
```

A passing gate remains valid until relevant inputs change. Stop rather than
commit or push when a required gate fails. Builds, packaging, signing, and
notarization belong to release workflows.

## Decide Documentation

Report either **Docs updated** when durable architecture, process, convention,
contract, or operator guidance changed, or **Docs not needed** when tests fully
specify a local behavior change. Update `CHANGELOG.md` only through an explicit
`update-changelog` or `prepare-release` flow.

## Audit And Report

Review the final diff and, when committing, the staged diff. Confirm it contains
only intended files, tests cover changed behavior, and no secrets, local data,
generated noise, or accidental changelog edits are included.

```text
DoD
- Scope: <change and boundary>
- Tests: <command and result>
- Typecheck/lint: <result or not applicable>
- Visual: <result or not applicable>
- Docs: <updated and why, or not needed>
- Worktree: <intended files only, or unrelated files preserved>
```

# Korus Frontend Development

Use this skill for renderer work: Vue components, Element Plus controls, chat
rendering, app shell, agent/team/Bench surfaces, artifact panes, themes, and
frontend tests.

## First Read

Read `docs/frontend.md` before editing UI. Read `docs/testing.md` before adding
or updating component tests.

## Principles

- Split UI into small named components with one clear job.
- Keep views thin. Views coordinate state and compose components.
- Keep raw Codex payloads out of renderer components; render app-owned state.
- Use typed props and emits for every component.
- Use Element Plus for standard controls when practical.
- Use semantic CSS variables for product colors and repeated design-system
  spacing, radii, shadows, typography, and diff values. Keep genuinely
  component-specific geometry local.
- Use `docs/codex.png` for the shell direction.
- Keep operational UI dense, quiet, and scannable.
- Avoid nested cards and decorative layouts.
- Prevent layout jumps during streaming, loading, approvals, and artifact pane
  changes.

## Reuse Audit

Before creating or styling a picker, menu, dialog, list, popover, settings
layout, button pattern, operation state, or icon control:

1. Read `docs/frontend.md` through **Canonical UI primitives**.
2. Search `client/vue/src/shared/` and `client/vue/src/components/` for the interaction and
   product concept, including existing wrappers and tests.
3. Reuse or extend the canonical primitive. A product wrapper may configure
   copy, slots, placement, and domain events; it must delegate the shared
   interaction and visual behavior.
4. If no primitive fits, put a genuinely reusable primitive under
   `client/vue/src/shared/`, add it to the inventory, and cover its public behavior in
   an isolated test. Keep one-off product composition in `client/vue/src/components/`.

The audit is complete when the implementation imports the matching primitive,
or the handoff identifies the concrete contract mismatch that required a new
one. Do not infer non-reuse from a component's historical product-specific
name; inspect its contract first.

## Tests And Verification

- Add or update colocated component tests when a component contract changes.
- Test components in isolation when behavior is local.
- Assert rendered output, emitted events, disabled states, selected state, and
  visible status changes.
- For shared rendering behavior, run the broad relevant test gate once scripts
  exist.
- For visual changes, run the app and check screenshots when tooling exists.

name: korus-live-preview
description: Use when interactively dogfooding Korus from a worktree, with isolated Electron state, realistic fixtures, reload persistence, or branch-local backend changes.

# Korus Live Preview

Run the current worktree's real Electron renderer and daemon with isolated app
state. Use representative domain data and meaningful edge states. Automated tests
remain a separate gate from interactive product evaluation.

## Prepare the preview

1. Read `docs/testing.md` and, for visible UI, `docs/frontend.md`.
2. Inspect the worktree and choose the workflow states to exercise. Seeds must
   match current app-owned schemas.
3. Create a uniquely named temporary home outside the repository. Put the seed at
   `<preview-home>/state.json` (migrated on first start) or write `roster.json` and
   `settings.json` directly. Never use the user's normal Korus home.
4. For provider-dependent workflows, copy only the normal installation's
   `codex-home/auth.json` into the isolated home's `codex-home/auth.json` with
   restrictive permissions. Never read or print its contents. Otherwise let the
   user authenticate in the isolated preview.
5. Build the daemon with `npm run build:backend`, then start Electron in a
   persistent exec session using the pinned runtime below. Pass
   `--user-data-dir=<preview-home>/electron` to isolate Chromium state as well as
   backend state. Shared UI lives in `client/vue`.

The preview home contains synthetic state and may contain credentials. Keep it
out of Git and remove it after the session. Record the home, worktree and owned
process/session IDs together; cleanup must target only those resources.

## Pin the runtime

Inherited `APP_BACKEND_COMMAND`, `APP_BACKEND_ARGS`, `APP_BACKEND_SOCKET` and
`APP_BACKEND_MODE` can select another installation or daemon. The root dev command
pins the built backend executable and arguments. For an isolated preview, use:

```bash
APP_HOME=<preview-home> \
APP_BACKEND_MODE=bundled \
APP_BACKEND_SOCKET=<preview-home>/daemon.sock \
APP_BACKEND_COMMAND=<absolute-node-path> \
APP_BACKEND_ARGS=<absolute-worktree>/client/backend/dist/daemon.mjs,--stdio \
APP_BACKEND_WATCH_FILE= \
npm run start:electron -- --user-data-dir=<preview-home>/electron
```

Root `npm run dev` remains the normal Electron development command.
Choose installed SDK packages by default (`CODEX_APP_SDK_SOURCE=0`); use source
linking only when explicitly testing SDK source integration.

For a repeatable automated Design workflow, run:

```bash
npm run build:backend
node scripts/verify-design-workspace.mjs <evidence-directory>
```

This launches its own Electron shell and daemon, exercises authored designs,
writes a check report and screenshots, and cleans up its temporary home. `--live`
also submits a real provider brief and consumes provider usage.

Browser component fixtures in `client/vue/src/components/__tests__/fixtures/`
remain useful for isolated DOM and layout checks. They do not prove desktop
preload, daemon, native behavior or provider integration.

## Drive the real shell

Use the `korus-computer-use` procedure and Korus Computer Use tools for interactive
macOS control. Confirm the window belongs to the isolated profile before acting.
For automated runtime checks, follow the existing Electron smoke workflows with
Playwright. Allocate any CDP/Vite port through port `0`, bind it to loopback, and
retry allocation after `EADDRINUSE`; never stop another agent's server.

Navigate through the actual feature entry point. Confirm the seeded state is
visible, exercise meaningful transitions, and reload when persistence matters.
If state is missing, check seed validity, the owning daemon snapshot, executable
provenance, then renderer adoption. Fix failures at their owning boundary.
Keep subjective product evaluation with the user and state what is synthetic.

## Close the session

Stop only this preview's owned processes. Validate the exact temporary home path
before removing it, including copied authentication. Confirm Git contains no
preview state, credentials, build noise or generated screenshots. Report automated
gates separately from interactive and native evidence.

description: Use when adding tests, fixing failing tests, raising coverage, changing IPC/app contracts, testing Vue components in isolation, or verifying Korus desktop behavior.

# Korus Testing And Coverage

Use this skill when adding tests, fixing failing tests, raising coverage, or
changing contracts.

## First Read

Read `docs/testing.md` before changing tests or testable behavior.
Apply its mandatory **Test Value Gate** before adding, modifying, or retaining a
test; if the protected regression cannot be named and made red through the
owning public seam, the test does not belong.

## Principles

- Test observable behavior and app contracts, not implementation details.
- Never add fixed real-time waits to Vue tests or their browser helpers, across
  desktop, console, mobile web and website. Use observable conditions, deferred
  events, or fake-clock advances for debounce/deadline behavior. Sleeps and
  `waitForTimeout` are forbidden.
- Match test scope to risk.
- Use focused tests while iterating, then run the full relevant gate.
- For provider integration, fake the public Codex app SDK or Claude Agent SDK
  and exercise the real Korus adapter/backend. For application integration, fake
  the unified backend and exercise real app state and representative mounted UI.
  Use the fixtures and ownership rules in `docs/testing.md`.
- For provider-independent services, test their own external boundary: Electron
  shell, filesystem, git, clocks, and OS dialogs.
- Prefer realistic component interaction over mutating internals directly.
- Extend existing owner-boundary workflows first. A shared component, helper,
  reducer or adapter does not automatically need its own test suite; apply the
  Test Value Gate before adding one.
- If focused tests pass but broader verification fails, reproduce and fix the
  broader failure.

## Component Tests

- Use Vitest, Vue Test Utils, and jsdom.
- Co-locate component tests in `__tests__/` folders.
- Use the real Element Plus plugin for controls.
- Test components in isolation when the behavior belongs to that component.
- Assert visible text, aria labels, button states, emitted payloads, selected
  rows, and status changes.
- Keep snapshots rare and explicit.

## Coverage Triage

- Use coverage to find missing risk, not to pad arbitrary lines.
- Prioritize missed branches in protocol adapters, IPC, persistence, reducers,
  tool/approval rendering, diff rendering, filesystem/git behavior, Bench, and
  teams.
- Prefer tests around public behavior before adding test-only seams.
- Gate every workspace on exactly 85% statements; report lines, branches, and
  functions without blocking thresholds. Preserve the measured surface.
- Coverage complements mandatory meaningful behavioral/regression tests and
  owning-boundary verification; it cannot replace them.
- Quality CI owns coverage on every branch push. Release CI independently runs
  ordinary tests without coverage against installed SDK packages; follow
  `prepare-release` rather than duplicating its gates locally.

## Standard Gates

Prefer these commands once scripts exist:

```bash
npm test
npm run test:ai
npm run test:coverage
npm run lint
npm run build
```

Prefer `npm run test:ai` for an unfiltered agent-driven suite. It keeps Vitest
summaries and failures while suppressing passing-test noise.

If a command is not available yet, report that directly in the handoff.
