# Hosted server

`backend/` owns hosted ingestion, authentication and reporting APIs. `frontend/`
owns the private admin console. `deploy/` contains portable Docker services and
`scripts/` owns image packaging and end-to-end server checks. The mobile and Electron clients are independent of the hosted frontend.

The console owns its Vue controls, theme and assets, and imports no client code.
Chart.js/vue-chartjs render analytics using the pure configuration and palette in
core, shared with desktop. Each renderer adapts its own data and accessible tooltips.

The server uses shared `@workspace/core` contracts and canonical UI primitives,
product metadata and assets from the app repository. Those shared inputs must be
packaged or transferred explicitly when extracting this directory into another
repository. Private host configuration and credentials belong in operator tooling.

## Hosted daily collector

`server/backend/src/collector` is an independently bundled Node service. It imports the
closed shared telemetry contract and PostgreSQL client, never the desktop daemon,
provider runtimes or companion relay. Dependency/AST lint enforces both directions
of this boundary. Building the desktop does not start or configure this service.

Build with `npm run build -w @workspace/server-backend`. The explicit
`npm run migrate -w @workspace/server-backend` command applies versioned,
transactional migrations under an externally supplied migration role. Ingestion
does not perform DDL. `npm run start -w @workspace/server-backend --
serve <operator-config.json>` starts the listener only after its tables are accessible.
Both commands read `TELEMETRY_DATABASE_URL` at runtime; it is never compiled into a
bundle. The private operator JSON supplies `listenHost`, `listenPort` and an
optional list of exact `trustedProxies` IP addresses. Database roles, credentials,
listener/routing configuration and TLS termination belong outside Git. PostgreSQL
18 or later supplies the transaction deadline used by the connection pool.

The versioned ingestion route accepts only JSON with the shared closed schema.
Its byte cap applies before UTF-8 decoding or parsing, including chunked bodies.
Hourly reports are accepted for any historical UTC hour through the current hour.
Legacy daily reports retain their completed-day contract. There is no historical
upload cutoff: `install_days`, `usage_daily` and the minimal
`installs` registry have no age-based expiry. The registry preserves the reporting
bucket of the first successfully committed submission, even when an older reporting
date arrives later; it does not claim an installation date.

Each replacement uses one PostgreSQL connection and transaction. The unique parent
upsert locks the install/day before replacing a single hourly bucket. The stored
hour markers include empty activity reports. The first hourly report replaces
legacy daily contributions; later legacy writes cannot overwrite hourly data.
Daily metrics sum the known hourly contributions before aggregation. Optional
measured-turn counts and cost coverage distinguish partial subtotals from complete
totals; legacy reports infer coverage from their existing nullable measurements.
Missing hours or groups never erase measured contributions from other hours.
The same parent lock serializes concurrent processes as well as concurrent requests;
removed groups disappear, including replacement with empty usage. The registry
insert is in the same transaction. HTTP success follows commit. A lost
acknowledgement can be retried without incrementing counts; a failed transaction
preserves the prior snapshot. SQL stores typed columns, not rollup JSON blobs.

Admission uses the socket peer unless it exactly matches an operator-configured
proxy; only then is a single validated `X-Real-IP` trusted. Forwarding lists and
missing/invalid trusted-proxy addresses are rejected. Source limits are 60 requests
per rolling minute with a ten-request burst, independently of the thirty requests
per installation per rolling hour. Rate-limit maps each hold at most 4096 live
keyed hashes with a process-random key; only expired entries can be reclaimed.
Nothing exports or persists this state. There are at most twenty in-flight request
handlers and 128 connections, with bounded body, statement, lock and transaction
deadlines. A client-side query deadline also bounds lost database replies; failed
transactions discard their connection after bounded rollback. Limit responses have
a bounded `Retry-After`. Random UUIDs and anonymous rate limits do not authenticate
installations or establish trustworthy downloads.

The collector has no request/access logger. Application failures emit JSON lines
with a timestamp, service, operation, recognized error code and an authored cause
and description. Database lock deadlines, missing migrations, permission failures,
connection failures and listener conflicts remain distinguishable without printing
raw error messages, stacks, SQL, parameters, addresses, installation identifiers,
request headers or bodies. Unknown errors identify the failed operation with an
`unexpected_error` cause and bounded application filename/line positions when
available; full stack traces and host paths remain excluded. Expected
invalid/unauthorized requests are not logged.
HTTP failures retain generic responses; recoverable database errors do not terminate
the process. Database logging, reverse-proxy logs and upstream infrastructure are
separate operator boundaries:
they must also suppress addresses, identifiers, query parameters and bodies before
the production no-IP-retention promise is verified. A local test cannot establish
that deployment guarantee.

The backend collector tests start disposable real `postgres:18.3-alpine`
containers with ephemeral loopback ports; Docker must be running. Repeat with
`npm run test -w @workspace/server-backend`. Setting
`TELEMETRY_COLLECTOR_EVIDENCE` to an untracked output file retains sanitized HTTP
status/count evidence. The workflow checks concurrent replacement across server
instances, rollback/connection loss, lost acknowledgements, exact limits, bounded
admission and retention of old accepted history. The executable build test also
proves operator-secret canaries do not enter the generated bundle.

## Private telemetry aggregates

The standalone bundle's `read <external-json-file>` mode is a separate process
using `telemetry_read`, never the ingestion pool or desktop runtime. Its runtime
JSON supplies `listenHost`, `listenPort`, `consoleOrigin` and `accessTokenFile`;
`TELEMETRY_DATABASE_URL` supplies the read-only database connection outside Git.
Startup checks schema readiness without DDL. Both executable modes share bounded
PostgreSQL timeouts, generic HTTP failures and the same privacy-safe diagnostics.

The private console uses a single `admin` operator account. Its password comes
from `BACKEND_ADMIN_PASSWORD` in an operator-managed, owner-only `.env` file
outside Git. Compose injects it only into the separate `auth` process, which has
no database credential or database network. Passwords must be at least 16
characters and at most 1,024 UTF-8 bytes; the process derives a salted scrypt hash
at startup. No operator credential is baked into images or browser assets.

The auth service keeps at most 128 opaque random sessions in memory for eight
hours. Cookies are host-only, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict and Secure under HTTPS.
Logout revokes the session. Restarting auth invalidates all sessions; changing
the private `.env` password requires recreating the auth container. Login and logout require the exact configured Origin. Login has a
global ten-attempt/minute budget and at most two concurrent scrypt operations;
rate state contains no IP addresses. Errors never echo credentials or cookies.

The console uses Vue Router history routes. Authentication guards resolve the
server session before rendering login or protected reports; an unavailable
authentication service produces a retryable state. Login return paths are
limited to the console report routes. The proxy also enforces authentication on
direct report URLs.

The proxy checks sessions before serving console HTML or
`/v1/telemetry/metrics`. Unauthenticated HTML redirects to `/login`; metrics return
401 without a browser password challenge. The login document and its static
assets are public. The proxy injects a separate private service bearer on the
internal metrics hop, while the API virtual host remains anonymous ingestion
only. Database credentials and the service token never enter browser assets or
responses. Supply a distinct 32–256 character URL-safe random service token
through `TELEMETRY_READ_ACCESS_FILE` and the exact HTTPS console origin (scheme,
host and optional port, without trailing slash/path) through
`TELEMETRY_CONSOLE_ORIGIN`. Internal metrics callers may omit Origin; any supplied
Origin must exactly match. The explicit
`TELEMETRY_CONSOLE_ALLOW_LOOPBACK_HTTP=1` option accepts HTTP only for a loopback
console origin in isolated local tests; production leaves it unset or zero.

The read endpoint accepts inclusive `from`/`to` calendar days, an optional IANA
`timeZone` (UTC when omitted), driver `provider` and exact full-name `model` filters and a boolean
`groupServiceTiers` option. The console supplies the viewer browser timezone and
includes today by default, using reports received so far. It rejects
unknown/duplicate filters, future viewer days and ranges longer than 3,660 days
instead of clipping results. Older retained ranges remain available. Model choices
come from nonzero recorded usage within the selected date/provider scope,
independently of the selected model.
At most four aggregate statements execute concurrently; excess work receives 429
with a one-second Retry-After. Database lock/statement deadlines yield generic 503
responses. Responses are not cached. The weekly top-ten ranking contains usage totals and
turn shares for anonymous installations in the final seven selected days, ranked
by turns. Ranks apply only within the response; installation identifiers never
leave the read service. Shares use all turns in the same filtered weekly scope,
including installations outside the top ten.

`core/src/telemetry-metrics.ts` is the browser-safe read contract. Cards use the
range's end day and global activity, independent of usage filters: cumulative
participating identities through that day, DAU, distinct trailing-seven WAU,
distinct trailing-30 MAU, and distinct calendar-month-to-date activity. Daily first
reports use the registry's first reported bucket. Empty-usage days contribute to
activity; multiple models cannot multiply it. Availability and last receipt time
are global so the console can show the latest received reporting day.

The single statement in `server/backend/src/collector/metrics.sql` supplies every API
section from one committed snapshot. All counts and decimal costs are exact
strings, including sums beyond JavaScript's safe integer range. Known token
subtotals include measured and unmeasured turn counts; input plus output totals
retain every known contribution. Legacy reports infer measured turns from their
nullable token fields. Cache share and its non-cache-read remainder use only
matched input/cache-read pairs from the same hourly or legacy daily report, with
zero denominators returning null.
That remainder can include cache creation; it is not a fresh-input pricing claim.
Hourly usage, activity and first-report buckets are assigned to viewer days by
their UTC hour start, including across daylight-saving changes. Legacy date-only
reports and first-report records retain their original date; no hour is inferred.
Fractional-offset zones use the hour-start day because finer timing is unavailable.
Weekly buckets start Monday in the viewer calendar and include only selected days.
Token charts stack known input and output contributions, matching the known token
total even when coverage is partial. Known cost subtotals sum without repricing;
explicit cost coverage preserves partial estimates through hourly and daily
aggregation. All-unknown and empty buckets have null cost,
with explicit complete/partial/unavailable/empty coverage. Missing spend is never
zero. Usage model rows are ordered by provider/model/tier and expose aggregates only.
Sparse model-day series retain the same grouping and weighted timing arithmetic
for model usage trends and performance comparisons; absent timing samples remain
unavailable.

The executable seed is
`server/backend/src/collector/__tests__/fixtures/metrics-seed.sql`. Apply it only to a
migrated disposable database. The owner workflow prepares the exact API SQL with
`PREPARE dashboard_example(date,date,text,text,boolean,text) AS <metrics.sql>`, then executes
`EXECUTE dashboard_example('2026-10-18','2026-10-24',NULL,NULL,false,'UTC')`. Expected global
cards are 6 participating identities, DAU 3, WAU 4, MAU 5 and calendar-month actives
4. Known input plus output totals 700 tokens, measured cache share is 0.55, and known cost is
1.5 USD with two unknown groups. The 2020 seed contributes another 1,100 tokens.
Run `TELEMETRY_METRICS_EVIDENCE=<external-evidence-file> npm run test -w
@workspace/server-backend -- src/collector/__tests__/metrics.spec.ts` to record repeatable
aggregate JSON while verifying SQL/API parity, private access, corrections,
unknowns, exact large integers and bounded database failure against real Postgres.

Run `npm run dev:console` from the repository root, or `npm run dev` in
`server/frontend`, for the loopback console with Vue hot reload on port 58191.
Its `/auth` and `/v1` requests proxy to a private local upstream on port 58192;
`TELEMETRY_CONSOLE_DEV_UPSTREAM` can select another operator-managed upstream.
Authentication and data access stay in that upstream, outside browser assets.

Build the portable private console with `npm run build:console`. The static
artifact is `server/frontend/dist`; supply its absolute directory privately through
`TELEMETRY_CONSOLE_DIRECTORY`. API/console hosts, exact console origin, trusted
edge configuration and viewer credentials remain external proxy inputs. The
browser uses the console's protected same-origin `/v1/telemetry/metrics` route;
there is no API host, service token or database credential to configure in a
browser bundle. No Vite environment prefix or dotenv directory is enabled for
this entry point. `npm run build:server` builds both hosted workspaces. The local browser app
has its own build command.

## Telemetry container operations

`server/deploy/compose.yaml` runs a separate collector, private PostgreSQL
18 database, migration/grant jobs, read-only metrics process, backup worker and minimal routing proxy. No
service joins the companion relay. Only the proxy publishes a port, bound to an
operator-supplied private interface behind an HTTPS edge. Database and collector
networks are internal; the proxy has no database-network membership. PostgreSQL
uses a project-scoped named volume mounted at its versioned data-directory parent.
Restart policies, memory/CPU/process limits and health gates bound the stack.
The collector handles database restarts; Compose also restarts it after explicit
database restart operations. Health failures require operator monitoring; Compose
restart policies alone do not restart a running unhealthy process.

Build the image with `node server/scripts/package.mjs <local-image-tag>`. Its
temporary Docker context contains only the standalone bundle, runtime adapter and
Dockerfile. The checkout, dependency tree, environment files and operator inputs
are not sent to Docker. Node, PostgreSQL and nginx base images are digest pinned;
review supported versions/security updates before deployment. The collector image
runs without root, capabilities or a writable root filesystem. No credentials,
external routes, TLS material or operator configuration are image layers.

Copy `server/deploy/operator.env.example` to an operator-managed location
outside Git and replace every placeholder. Select a unique Compose project name,
an unused private container subnet, and distinct collector/metrics/auth/proxy addresses within
it. Reserve all four addresses for this stack. Supply distinct random database-role
passwords as newline-terminated secret files, the server-only console password
in the private operator environment, the reviewed console build directory, and a
trusted-edge nginx include. Keep their
parent directory owner-only. Compose file-backed secrets retain host permissions:
make the mounted files readable by their receiving container UID without opening
the parent directory to other host users. The backup directory must be writable
by the PostgreSQL image UID/GID (70:70), mode 0700, and reside on protected storage.
Do not store these inputs, resolved Compose output, archives or inventories in Git.
Resolved Compose output contains the runtime console password and must not be
printed into shared logs.
Ordinary Compose file secrets are bind mounts, not an encrypted secret store.

Use `docker compose --env-file <external-env-file> -p <isolated-project> -f
server/deploy/compose.yaml config` to review the resolved deployment
privately, then `up -d --wait` with the same options. Startup waits for database
readiness, applies versioned migrations under `telemetry_migrate`, then grants only
required table operations before admitting HTTP. Ingestion cannot create schema,
delete active days, change registry history or read migration state. The backup
role has SELECT only; the dashboard role has SELECT only on data tables.
The migration role has no cluster/role creation or superuser capability. Bootstrap
roles run only for a new data volume: replacing a password file does not rotate a
database role password. Perform role credential rotation privately and coordinate
all consumers. Schema upgrades require rerunning migrations and grants explicitly
with the new image before restarting ingestion; `up` reruns completed jobs.

The proxy accepts only the ingestion route on the configured API host and serves
the separate console host behind server-side session authentication. This is an
internal HTTP hop, never a public cleartext listener. The external HTTPS edge must
preserve the virtual host and securely convey client addresses. Its private nginx
include must trust only the actual TLS-edge peer ranges using `set_real_ip_from`,
`real_ip_header` and an appropriate `real_ip_recursive` setting; never trust all
peers. An empty include is suitable only when the proxy receives the source
connection directly. The proxy replaces forwarding headers and strips cookies,
authorization and user-agent before ingestion. The collector trusts only this
stack's explicit proxy address. The read service shares the private database and
frontend networks under a separate SELECT-only role; its console route keeps
server-side viewer authentication. The ingestion proxy rejects every other API
route.

The collector, metrics, auth and migration containers retain application diagnostics
through Docker's local logging driver, rotating three files of up to 5 MB per
service. Nonblocking delivery uses a bounded buffer; records may be dropped under
output pressure. Inspect them with `docker compose` using the same private operator
inputs and project name, followed by `logs --tail 100 collector metrics auth migrate`.
These records cover individual application failures and lifecycle events, without
periodic request summaries. PostgreSQL, nginx and backup/grant infrastructure logs
remain disabled. There are no access logs, request caches or disk-buffered ingestion
bodies. PostgreSQL statement/parameter/connection logs and extensions are disabled;
nginx access/error logging is disabled globally. Health checks use
configuration/readiness only and produce no request records. The database and
backups intentionally contain installation UUIDs and numeric rollups, never source
addresses or conversation content. Monitor health/exit state, backup freshness and
disk capacity alongside application diagnostics. Set `TELEMETRY_LOGGING_EVIDENCE`
to an external JSON file when running `npm run test:server:infrastructure`
to retain the sanitized records from its real database-failure probe.
Do not enable packet capture, debug logs, SQL audit extensions or request tracing
on this route in production.

Before Ship, privately verify the effective database configuration, HTTPS edge,
upstream CDN/WAF/security/access logs, crash/support collectors and their backups.
They must retain no source addresses, headers, request bodies, URL identifiers or
queries for this telemetry path. Confirm direct collector/database ports are
unreachable and the private console cannot bypass authentication. Verify Docker
capacity, image provenance, filesystem permissions, TLS, routing and restore
monitoring in that environment. Local containers prove only the supplied stack;
production no-IP-storage verification remains a separate Ship precondition.

The backup worker makes consistent custom-format `pg_dump` archives daily and
checks seven-day expiry hourly, including when dumps fail. A copy expires at
604800 seconds; the sweep removes it on the next hourly check. Dumps have a
ten-minute wall deadline and bounded database queries. Only successful dumps are
atomically published, with private file permissions; stale partial dumps expire
as well. Health becomes unhealthy if rotation or successful backup is overdue.
Archive timestamps describe backup creation, never a data-retention cutoff:
accepted daily rollups and the installation registry stay indefinitely in primary
storage and every complete backup. All replicas, snapshots and off-host archive
copies must apply the same seven-day expiry, including while this worker is down.
Operator monitoring must catch a stopped worker or failed deletion. No script
truncates live history. These daily logical backups have up to one day of data
loss; they do not provide continuous WAL recovery.

Run `docker compose ... run --rm backup once` for an on-demand archive and
`docker compose ... run --rm backup rotate` for immediate expiry. Restore only a
trusted archive from the same service: PostgreSQL restore can execute SQL authored
by the source database owner. Create a separate empty recovery database owned by
`telemetry_migrate`, then run `docker compose ... run --rm -e
PGDATABASE=<recovery-database> restore <archive-name>`. The restore refuses the
primary database and nonempty destinations, restores in one transaction with
original owners/ACLs omitted, and never changes the primary snapshot. Validate
counts/aggregates and oldest retained days before any separately authorized
recovery cutover. Reapply grants before serving a recovered database; restoration
must not resurrect expired backup copies in other storage.

`npm run test:server:infrastructure` builds the real isolated image and
exercises the disposable Compose stack, role denials, HTTP through nginx,
restart/recreation persistence, exact expiry boundaries, failed dumps and isolated
restore including old history. It removes its containers, networks and volumes.
Set `TELEMETRY_STACK_EVIDENCE` to an untracked output file for sanitized results.

Run `npm run test:server:e2e` for the console browser workflow in
`server/frontend/src/__tests__/console-e2e.spec.mjs` (skipped without a Docker engine). It starts a disposable local stack without
database restart, backup-expiry or restore exercises. Its fixture uses synthetic
credentials and never reads an operator environment or connects to a deployed host.

The console workflow connects an isolated desktop-owned profile through the real
settings/activity RPC, SQLite ledger and `TelemetryUploadService` to that stack.
Its local fault receiver forwards canonical bytes and discards an acknowledgement
after commit. Restart and repeated window notifications must preserve one logical
day; the private console checks the resulting counts and a complete replacement.
Time, desktop lifecycle notifications and provider observations are scripted. Provider
normalization remains covered by the Claude/Codex ledger fixtures, not by live
provider calls. Set `TELEMETRY_PROFILE_EVIDENCE` to an external JSON file and
`TELEMETRY_DASHBOARD_EVIDENCE` to an external screenshot directory to retain this
evidence. These artifacts contain synthetic installation IDs and local payloads;
keep them out of deployment images and Git.

## Telemetry Ship handoff

Local validation does not authorize production activation. The operator must
review the intended image and console build, supply the external inputs in
`operator.env.example`, and complete these checks before enabling delivery:

- Confirm supported Docker/Compose and pinned image availability, an unused
  private subnet, memory/CPU/process capacity and durable disk capacity for
  indefinitely retained history. Set monitoring for disk growth, health failures,
  overdue backups/rotation and failed restore drills.
- Supply separate least-privilege credentials, private console authentication and
  the internal read-service token outside Git. Verify unauthenticated console
  requests reveal no metrics, anonymous writes cannot read, and database/read
  services cannot be reached directly from the public network.
- Verify HTTPS routing and exact console-origin rules using privately supplied
  host configuration. Desktop releases embed the `APP_TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT` build
  secret as a public default; keep it absent until activation is approved. A runtime
  value overrides the bundled endpoint, and an explicitly blank value disables it.
  The console build uses a relative authenticated route and contains no operator credential.
- Inspect effective collector, PostgreSQL, proxy, TLS edge and every upstream
  CDN/WAF/security/access/crash-support logging path, including external copies
  and backups. Prove the telemetry route retains no connection IP, request
  headers, identifier-bearing URL/query or body. Local no-log assertions do not
  establish this production fact. Resolve any mismatch before publishing the
  no-IP-storage promise or releasing an enabled endpoint.
- Verify seven-day expiry for every backup/replica copy, including worker
  downtime, and perform an isolated restore with old retained history. Live
  rollups and the minimal installation registry have no age-based cleanup.
- Publish and verify the approved privacy policy and Analytics guidance before
  a released app can offer active sharing. Recheck onboarding, first-upgrade and
  Settings policy links against that published version. Coordinate the separately
  approved endpoint activation and signed app release. An unset choice remains off
  until the desktop notice enables sharing after one foreground minute, the user
  closes it, or the General settings toggle enables it. Saved opt-outs stay off.

Record production privacy verification, deployment, policy publication, signed app
release and actual public availability as separate delivery evidence. A local
unsigned build, synthetic provider fixture or disposable-container trace proves
none of those facts. Shipping requires explicit authorization for each action.

# Korus website

This contains the static landing page and VitePress documentation for [meetkorus.dev](https://meetkorus.dev).

## Local preview

Use the repository's Node 26 reference toolchain, with the exact version pinned
in [`.nvmrc`](../.nvmrc) and npm setup covered in the
[development requirements](../README.md#development).

```bash
npm run docs:build
node website/build.mjs
npx vite dist/website --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4173 --strictPort
```

Then open <http://127.0.0.1:4173>.

Product metadata comes from `core/src/product.json`. The landing-page build
expands the product name, canonical URL, and GitHub download links; VitePress reads the
same definition and sends `__PRODUCT_DOWNLOAD_URL__` guide links to the platform chooser. Preview
the built artifact so the name and documentation are both available.

## Documentation

The public privacy policy is authored in `privacy/index.html` and published at
`/privacy/`. The website build expands its shared product metadata and includes
it in the static artifact beside the landing page and guide.
Keep the policy's contact links inside Cloudflare's `email_off` comments so
the public email address remains accessible without JavaScript.

Optional telemetry has a release gate: privately verify the collector, reverse
proxy and every upstream delivery/security/access-log path retain no IP addresses
or report content before publishing that promise or activating a sending endpoint.
Local browser, container and fixture checks do not establish production privacy.
Publish and verify the matching `/privacy/` policy and Analytics guide before the
telemetry-enabled desktop release can offer opt-in. Website publication, endpoint
activation and app release require their separate approved Ship actions; building
these assets authorizes none of them.

The public user guide lives in `website/docs/` and uses VitePress with a
customized default theme. The navigation follows Getting started, Providers,
Workflows, Features, Reference, and Troubleshooting. Internal engineering notes
stay in the repository's top-level `docs/` directory and are not published.

Describe product behavior directly in the public guide. Do not add release
planning notices, upcoming-version labels, or comparisons between `main` and
the published app. Keep release status and version history in release notes.

Run from the repository root:

```bash
npm run docs:dev
```

Open the `/docs/` URL reported by VitePress. Edit the Markdown pages and keep
the sidebar in `website/docs/.vitepress/config.mts` in sync. Search uses the
local page index and requires no hosted search service. The theme reuses the
landing page's public assets and supplies light and dark tokens.

Build, check, and preview the complete static website:

```bash
npm run test:docs
npm run docs:check
npx vite dist/website --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4173 --strictPort
```

Visit <http://127.0.0.1:4173/docs/>. `test:docs` builds the site and checks the
generated links, anchors, asset paths, and exclusion of authoring files.
`npm run docs:preview` previews just the VitePress production output after
`npm run docs:build`.

Use a file extension on raw HTML card links so direct loads work on the static
host. Keep VitePress's dead-link checking enabled. The site uses `/docs/` as
its base path and standard `.html` page URLs, so nginx needs no SPA rewrite
for documentation routes.

## Product preview

The website uses white and neutral-gray surfaces, near-black text, blue accents,
and system UI typography. Films keep charcoal title cards and a quiet accent palette;
green and red communicate success and defects. Shared film branding comes
from `videos/product.mjs`, including the closing URL from product metadata.

All Korus marks use the exact geometry in `client/electron/assets/icon.svg`. The
website and Vue branding PNGs share a rounded web presentation; desktop icons
remain full-square. Composite the canonical vector into thumbnails, the social

### Local AI voice comparison

The Delegation comparison uses full BF16 Qwen3-TTS 1.7B on Apple Silicon through
MLX, conditioned on the two approved synthetic male audition samples. Model and
library versions are pinned in `videos/local-voices.json` and
`videos/requirements-voice.txt`.

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12 .app-dev/video-tts
uv pip install --python .app-dev/video-tts/bin/python -r videos/requirements-voice.txt
.app-dev/video-tts/bin/python videos/generate-local-narration.py
.app-dev/video-tts/bin/python videos/check-local-narration.py
node videos/render-voice-comparison.mjs
npx vite videos/local/voice-comparison --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4189 --strictPort
```

Keep the approved `ming-american-male-raw.wav` and `ming-british-male-raw.wav`
references in `videos/local/voice-references/`, or pass `--references`.
Missing references fail explicitly; the generator never substitutes a descriptive
prompt. Each film is generated in one uninterrupted reference-conditioned call.
Never synthesize individual sentences independently: the same voice prompt and
seed did not preserve speaker identity in the rejected Ming exports. Ming's full
paragraph attempts also repeated or dropped copy, so those are not used.

The checker independently transcribes the entire take, rejects missing/repeated
words, aligns each caption to recognized word timestamps, and screens reference
and adjacent-line speaker similarity using [Resemblyzer](https://github.com/resemble-ai/Resemblyzer).
The 0.8 similarity floor is a local diagnostic screen, not a perceptual guarantee;
listen before publishing. SHA-256 provenance prevents stale checks from certifying
new audio. Both generation and checking run locally after model downloads.
Use `--voice american-male` or `--voice british-male`, optionally `--seed 43`, to
retry a whole take. Never retry only one line with a new speaker sample.
Focused checks: `node --test videos/narration.test.mjs` and
`.app-dev/video-tts/bin/python videos/narration-alignment.test.py`.

Both films use the same script and choreography, with visual timing aligned to
each take. The paced edit inserts silence between lines from the same approved
take, without regenerating lines or trimming natural breaths. A pitch-preserving
tempo adjustment makes speech 4% slower, with pauses approximately 10% longer
than the previous 40–41-second edit. Visuals and captions follow the adjusted timing; the final
screen is retained. To adjust pacing,
rerun only `node videos/render-voice-comparison.mjs`, not voice generation.
The assembler rejects stale
alignment, failed voice checks, and extreme timing outliers. All generated WAVs, provenance
JSON, MP4s, captions, and the comparison page stay in the ignored `videos/local/voice-comparison/` folder. Model caches and
the ignored virtual environment stay outside tracked source. The originals and
the macOS drafts are untouched; the two-voice comparison is not deployed.
Use Vite for the reviewer: its byte-range responses allow immediate video seeking;
Python's basic HTTP server can reset seeks to zero even after buffering the file.

## Deploy

### Manual downloads

The header and hero detect the visitor's platform without external scripts.
iPhone Download buttons open the App Store listing from
`core/src/product.json` (`companionAppStoreUrl`). The download chooser also
includes an explicit iPhone link without JavaScript. All desktop platforms
remain accessible: macOS Apple silicon, Windows x64 (unsigned),
and Linux x64 / ARM64 with DEB, RPM, and ZIP choices. Browser OS detection does
not infer CPU architecture; Linux always opens the explicit choices. Android,
iPad, ChromeOS, and unknown browsers open all downloads. The chooser also works
without JavaScript.

Public download URLs use `/releases/latest/download/<filename>` so they follow
GitHub's latest stable release without a version pin or website redeployment.
The build queries the public latest-release API and verifies asset names,
completed uploads, canonical URLs, and download responses before exposing links.
Missing formats link to `/releases/latest`; if no stable release exists, all
platforms fall back to `/releases`. API failures other than that missing-release
case stop the build rather than silently publishing incomplete download choices.

Prereleases remain accessible on GitHub but never replace stable download
targets. Stable promotion belongs to the release workflow, not the website.

The website-owned asset mapping in `downloads.mjs` follows the release contract:
`<slug>-macos-arm64.dmg`, `<slug>-win32-x64-setup.exe`,
`<slug>-win32-x64.zip`, and `<slug>-linux-{x64,arm64}.{deb,rpm,zip}`.
The macOS updater ZIP is not offered as a manual installer.
`npm run test:website` covers publication/link safeguards; browser checks cover
OS shortcuts, explicit architecture choices, and responsive layout.

### Website upload

The deploy helper first builds the landing page and generated documentation into
`dist/website/`, then streams that artifact over SSH, provisions the Let’s Encrypt
certificate if this is the first deploy, and installs the matching nginx site on the operator-supplied SSH host:

```bash
APP_WEBSITE_HOST=<operator-ssh-host> ./website/deploy.sh
```

Set `APP_WEBSITE_HOST` explicitly. Override `APP_WEBSITE_ROOT` or `APP_NGINX_CONFIG` when needed. The remote account must be able to run `sudo install`, `sudo nginx -t`, and `sudo systemctl reload nginx`.

The domain and storage root come from `core/src/product.json`; nginx templates
are rendered outside the public artifact. The host serves the website, downloads,
and releases from `/var/www/korus/{site,downloads,releases}`. Certificate renewal
uses `/var/www/korus/site` as its webroot.

Deployment verifies the GitHub release-page fallback as well as direct assets
before making server changes. It uploads only the website; it neither publishes
desktop releases nor changes their prerelease/stable status.

Keep the existing `/desktop/releases/darwin/arm64/RELEASES.json` feed and
`/desktop/downloads/korus-macos-arm64.dmg` installer unchanged. Their nginx
aliases and storage directories remain separate from the website. Any bridge
update requires a separately approved stable release; do not redirect the JSON
feed to `update.electronjs.org`, which uses a different format.

# Korus CLI

Diagnose Korus and get help from a coding agent, even when the desktop app cannot open.

```sh
npx korus-cli@latest doctor
npx korus-cli@latest triage
```

Requires Node.js 22 or newer. Runs independently of Electron and the Korus backend.

- **doctor** checks your installation, saved state and available connections. Each coding client has a section with its version, authentication status and home directory. It is read-only. Optional services and warnings do not cause a failing exit status; errors do. Use `--json` for structured output or `NO_COLOR=1` for plain text.
- **triage** gathers local diagnostics and opens an installed, authenticated client: Claude Code, Codex, then Antigravity. Describe the problem after the command, or use `--agent` to choose a client. Recovery actions require your approval. Use `--no-launch` to prepare diagnostics without opening a client.
- **logs** reads redacted logs; `--follow` streams new entries, including after log rotation. It works in terminals and pipes. Combine `--follow --json` for newline-delimited JSON. Use `--lines` for the initial tail and `--since` or `--agent` to filter entries.
- **support bundle** creates a local diagnostics folder for you to review before sharing. Logs require `--include-logs`. Nothing is uploaded.
- **backend status**, **backend start**, **backend restart**, and **backend stop** inspect or control an installed macOS background service. Changes require confirmation.
- **agents list** and **missions list** inspect live metadata when available and fall back to saved state. Use `--offline` to read saved state directly.

Run `npx korus-cli@latest --help` for all options. To install the `korus` command:

```sh
npm install --global korus-cli
korus doctor
```

Exit codes: `0` for success, empty results or a declined confirmation; `1` for an operational error; `2` for invalid usage or missing non-interactive confirmation; `130` for Ctrl+C; `143` for SIGTERM. Triage forwards the launched client’s exit status.

# Agent Isolation

Design note: the shared-checkout warning is **not implemented**. Today agent
creation permits several agents in one folder without a warning and no policy is
persisted. Treat everything below as direction until an isolation policy matrix is
agreed.

## Problem

An agent is attached to a folder, so two agents on one Git checkout mutate the same
files, index, branch and build outputs. Isolation choices appear in several places
(repository session creation, backlog assignment, duplicate/fork, automations, MCP
`create-agent`), and all are the same question: when should work share a checkout,
and when should Korus require or recommend isolation? Independent per-surface
warnings would produce inconsistent policy.

## Vocabulary

- **Checkout:** one working-tree folder with its files, index, branch and
  uncommitted changes. **Worktree:** another checkout of the same repository sharing
  objects and refs but not files or index. Worktrees are the intended isolation
  boundary for concurrent coding even though they are not perfect process isolation.
- **Shared checkout:** two or more open agents on the same checkout *at the same
  execution location*. Teams are organizational, not isolation boundaries; identical
  paths on different hosts are different checkouts; Quick Chats have no workspace.
- **Repository identity:** the credential-free remote identity when available,
  otherwise a stable local root.

## Agreed Direction

An explicit, user-driven action that would create another agent in a checkout used
by any open agent (every team, same location, working or idle) warns first, naming the
checkout and listing the conflicting agents with their teams, and explaining that
files, uncommitted changes, branch switches, commits, resets and outputs are shared.
The dialog has **Cancel** and **Continue** plus a radio group: ask again (default),
don't ask again for this repository, don't ask again for any repository. Suppression
must be reversible in Settings, with a discoverable reset for repository exceptions.

## Architecture Direction

Assessment lives in `daemon`, which owns agent state, locations, filesystem and Git
identity, persistence, MCP and automations. The renderer receives an app-owned
assessment (target kind, repository and checkout identity, sharing agents and teams,
same-location flag, safe/warnable/disallowed, applicable preference, available
alternatives such as a new worktree) and never infers checkout identity from path
strings. Confirmation and mutation use one authoritative decision path: a renderer
preflight alone would be bypassed by MCP, automations, remote clients and races.

## Open Questions

1. Do duplicate and fork (which often keep the folder on purpose) always warn, use
   different copy, or offer isolation inline?
2. Does the warning apply to plain folders, which have no remote identity for
   repository-level suppression?
3. Does "don't ask again for this repository" follow a repository across machines and
   clones, or only one execution location? How are exceptions listed and reset?
4. What must automations enforce (worktree-only, per-automation policy, or a blocked
   run with a resolution path; silently sharing an active checkout is the weakest)?
5. What does MCP `create-agent` do when its target checkout is in use? A model must
   not bypass a user safety preference.
6. Should Korus offer navigating to the existing agent instead of creating another?

Next step: resolve these into one policy matrix, define the backend contract and
persistence, then implement every creation surface against it.

# Choosing The Coding Agent

How Korus picks Codex, Claude Code or Antigravity for new work.

## Rules

- Providers are peers; any subset may be connected on a host. Installation, process
  health and authentication are distinct. Choices come from the owning host's
  `providerConnections`, never legacy enable flags or backend process health.
- With several connected engines, creation surfaces show a selector; with one, it is
  used automatically and the selector is hidden; with none, new work is rejected and
  Settings offers connection. Existing chats stay accessible.
- Surfaces differ in presentation, not policy. Dialogs (New agent, worktree,
  project, branch/work-item, repository URL) carry a conditional `BackendSelector`;
  direct actions (new session on main, open folder, Quick Chat, duplicate agent,
  new Mission) create immediately and let the user choose on the empty chat. An explicit selection
  carries through acquisition and progress dialogs. Assigning to an existing session
  never implies a provider change.
- **Duplicate** defaults to the source backend and accepts an explicit available backend;
  changing it applies the target provider’s defaults to the fresh agent. **Fork** keeps
  the source backend. **MCP creation** (`create-agent`,
  `create-project`) takes an optional backend defaulting to the caller's. Same-provider
  helpers inherit the caller's model, effort and explicit service tier; cross-provider
  creation uses the target provider's defaults instead.
- **Missions:** new workers inherit the main Mission agent's current provider,
  model, reasoning effort and service tier, not the assigned team member's profile.
  The first Mission agent starts from the selected orchestrator member. Tickets
  approval may persist an independent implementation provider, model and reasoning
  effort. Cross-provider workers use the target provider's defaults. The daemon
  validates provider availability and the selection against the host's filtered
  catalog before worktree creation and each worker launch. Implementation workers,
  including reused workers and retries, use that selection; the lead and Review
  retain their configuration and conversations.
- **Review:** the reviewer's provider is an independent choice (Claude can review
  Codex work and vice versa). The panel remembers provider, model, effort and
  automation preferences. `start_automatic_review` inherits the caller's
  provider/model/effort and uses saved preferences only for priority threshold and
  round limit. Changing provider never transfers provider-specific conversation IDs
  or incompatible model settings.
- Validation gives a clear error for an unavailable explicit provider instead of
  silently using another.

## Host Requirements

An operator can limit the model choices offered by desktop and mobile with
`$APP_HOME/requirements.json` (normally `~/.korus/requirements.json`). The daemon
reads this optional file at startup, independently of saved preferences, and never
rewrites it. Restart the daemon after editing it. Invalid JSON, unknown fields or
providers, and invalid model lists stop startup with an error.

For a demo that offers only Codex Luna:

```json
{
  "models": {
    "codex": ["gpt-6-luna"],
    "claude": [],
    "antigravity": []
  }
}
```

Entries match provider catalog model identifiers (`model` or `id`), not display
names. Omitted providers keep their full catalog; an empty list disables that
provider for new work while preserving its conversations. Settings cannot re-enable
a provider disabled by requirements. Filtered catalogs retain an allowed provider
default or select the first remaining model as the default. Catalog updates use the
same filter, so discovery cannot restore excluded choices. Each host owns its
requirements; remote clients receive the owning host's filtered catalog and
availability. The file controls Korus model choices, not the provider's own CLI or
native subagents.

## Switching Before The First Prompt

A fresh conversation can change backend from a composer-shelf control, even after
creation chose one. Eligibility means **a fresh conversation before its first
submitted prompt**, not merely an empty message list: loading, provider-session,
history-bearing forks and running conversations are not switchable. The persisted
`hasSubmittedPrompt` marker locks selection even if the first submission failed
before a session existed; restart clears it with the old session.

Switching is an app-owned operation that updates provider and compatible defaults
together and releases any eagerly created empty provider session (the renderer
cannot swap a label over another provider's session). It refreshes model catalog,
reasoning, permission and capability controls, clears incompatible defaults, keeps
draft text and attachments (revalidating attachment support), and keeps model IDs and
approval settings provider-scoped. Sending waits for an outstanding switch, and late
catalog responses from the former provider are ignored. Antigravity effort is encoded
in native model IDs; separate effort, thinking-budget and service-tier settings do
not apply.

## Connection State

`core/agent-backends` resolves connected providers and fresh-agent eligibility;
`AppShell` provides the choices once through `backend-selection`. `daemon` owns
connection observations, published in snapshots but never persisted: installation and
authentication are checked once per backend startup and cached, routine reads reuse
them, and explicit connect, install or home/runtime changes refresh them. A
provider-reported auth failure updates the observation immediately
(`provider.authenticationChanged`) without touching the saved enabled preference, and
new-work admission re-probes engines last seen disconnected, so a login completed
outside Korus is picked up on retry. There is no continuous monitoring; remote hosts
report their own connections.

- Manual choices are remembered per client and host; an unavailable remembered engine
  falls back for new work without overwriting the preference. Existing conversations,
  delegated work, duplicates without an explicit backend, forks and persisted automations
  keep their engine and never silently switch on auth loss. Automations persist their backend for filtering and
  execution (filtering uses a tool-free, non-persisted Claude query) and fail before
  provisioning when it is disconnected.
- Enablement is persisted separately (`providerEnabled`); availability requires
  installed, authenticated **and** enabled. Toggling never probes or signs out. A host
  rejects disabling its last available engine. With no available engine, startup shows
  setup even for an existing workspace; setup can enable an already-authenticated
  engine without another login. Disabling preserves histories, drafts, queues and
  running turns, blocks new work, and pending Korus prompts resume on re-enable.
  Credential renewal and sign-in stay with the provider runtimes.

Execution choices cross application and process boundaries as the shared `ExecutionSelection` value. Admission inputs may carry typed overrides; the owning host resolves those against the selected provider before execution. Provider policy and observed conversation settings remain separate. Runtime validation and provider adapters cover every selection field so additions require updating those boundaries. Saved selections are normalized on load, and the roster schema prevents older daemons from rewriting the migrated layout.

# Architecture

Korus is a desktop and mobile app for coordinating teams of coding agents
with native conversation and artifact rendering. It does not embed a terminal.
Provider runtimes (Codex app-server, Claude Agent SDK) run behind `daemon`; every
client renders app-owned state and provider-owned conversation frames.

Product identity (names, paths, MCP namespace) comes from `core/src/product.json`.
Implementation identifiers stay brand-neutral. Types, method names and event
unions live in `core/src/`; this document records only what the code cannot say:
ownership, invariants and the reasons behind them.

Quota pauses are conversation-scoped agent metadata. The owning daemon persists
known reset deadlines and the auto-resume preference, then submits one `continue`
after the reset through normal prompt admission. Provider adapters supply reset
metadata; the scheduler is provider-neutral. Manual prompts, replacement
conversations and closed agents cancel pending continuation. Desktop clients show
the same pending state above the composer; closing a client does not cancel it.

The hosted services are separate from the app runtime: `server/backend` owns the
collector, admin authentication and aggregate APIs; `server/frontend` owns the
private admin console. `server/deploy` and `server/scripts` own their portable
runtime and packaging. See [the hosted server](../server/README.md).

## Process Model

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UI["@workspace/vue UI"] <--> Preload <--> Main["Electron main"] <--> D["daemon"]
  D <--> State["APP_HOME state"]
  D <--> P["Codex app-server / Claude Agent SDK"]
  D <--> Git["git, files, MCP server"]
```

**Rule:** an operation that acts on a repository, agent, provider session, work
item, transcript or backend-owned path belongs in `daemon`. An operation that asks
the local desktop to show UI or use an OS affordance belongs in Electron main.

- `daemon` owns product state and its only writer, provider processes and
  protocols, approvals, git, files, worktrees, automations, work integrations,
  the MCP server and runtime state. Clients never read backend-owned paths: file
  previews are `agentId` requests, and absolute or `file://` transcript links are
  normalized to agent-relative paths or forwarded to the owning daemon.
- Electron main owns windows, menus, dialogs, deep links, native permission and
  speech helpers, packaged resource paths, and the stdio/socket client to
  `daemon`. It adopts snapshots returned by backend RPCs and never derives product
  state itself. `daemon` supplies a derived `ClientState` for the few native
  decisions that depend on product state (dialog defaults, display sleep).
- Deep links are an automation interface: `korus://new?prompt=…` and
  `korus://agents/<id>?prompt=…` submit by default (`submit=false` prefills the
  composer). Electron converts accepted URLs to typed `AppCommand`s; raw URLs never
  cross preload.
- The renderer owns visual state. It never talks to a provider, spawns tools,
  reads local files, or imports provider protocol types.
- Preload is a small typed bridge and the only renderer path to Electron.
- Several windows can be open at once. Each window is its own renderer with its own
  replica of the daemon's state and its own view state (selected agent, panes);
  `WindowRegistry` in Electron main tracks what belongs to a window. Daemon events,
  connection changes and update status fan out to every window. Commands about the
  current window (menu, deep links, debug fixtures) go to the focused one, and
  commands about an agent's browser or simulator go to the window that owns it. Native
  views exist once per agent: the first window to mount one owns it, other windows
  offer to move it, and a closed window gives its views up. Composer drafts are one per
  agent, relayed live through main so every window shows the same text. A window is
  always opened with an initial view state, so New Window and every "Open in New
  Window" entry share one call.
- A window has a scope. A workspace window shows everything. A team window shows one
  team with its sidebar and no rail. A feature window is the same for one feature, which
  is a team and a Git branch: its sidebar lists the team's agents on that branch as they
  are now, so agents added to it appear, with nothing that creates or opens anything
  else. Feature windows keep their own split layout. A Mission window shows one
  Mission's workbench and conversations without the rail or sidebar. An agent window shows one agent
  with no rail or sidebar; it is smaller and never restores or saves the workspace
  frame. Scoped windows ignore navigation they cannot show, never overwrite the team's
  saved split layout, and close when their team, agent, feature or Mission is deleted. The Close
  shortcut of an agent window closes the window, never the agent. Opening in a new
  window is a view, not a move: the source stays visible where it was. Windows are
  equal, with no special main window. Window > Show Workspace and a Dock click with
  only scoped windows open both bring a workspace window back. Each window is titled for
  what it shows, and the Window menu lists the windows by title so any of them can be
  brought forward (macOS lists them itself; elsewhere main builds the list). Deep links
  and captures go to a workspace window.
- Navigation keys follow what they move through: Control+Tab cycles agents (the feature's,
  in a feature window), Control+\` cycles teams in a workspace window, and Command+\`
  cycles windows through the Window menu, each reversed with Shift. Command+W closes the
  window, whatever it shows; closing an agent deletes it and takes Command+Shift+D. Closing
  a team is only in the team's own menu, behind a confirmation.
- The open windows are remembered and reopened at launch: for each, its scope, what it
  shows (team, agent or feature, and the selected agent of a workspace window) and its
  frame, listed from least to most recently focused so the last one opened is in front.
  The layout is rewritten shortly after any change and once more as the app quits, and it
  keeps what it had when the last window closes. A window whose team, agent or feature
  is gone is skipped, a feature keeps its remaining agents, and without anything usable
  the default workspace window opens.
- Each window reports the panes it has open per agent (right-panel tabs that carry nothing
  but where to look, and the pages of its Browser tabs) and main keeps the latest. A window
  opened from another starts with a copy of its source's panes and then drifts on its own;
  the layout file and a reload start a window from its own; a Browser moved to another
  window brings its pages with it. Tabs holding a file, diff, image, plan or subagent
  conversation stay in their window.

The local mobile simulator host owns device attachments and native command execution
in Electron. Its pane and provider-independent MCP tool share that authority;
[the MCP model](mcp.md#mobile-simulators) records the attachment and coordinate rules.
Normal video teardown settles pending reads with an ended result; cleanup is
idempotent and cannot stop a replacement view. Native stream failures remain errors.
Fold controls are exposed from the simulator's device type, independently of its
editable name. Desktop-only hinge changes close the old view and wait for the
active display to settle before capturing new dimensions and accepting touch.

Host capabilities are enforced in `daemon` as well as in the UI: a persisted
desktop preference cannot enable a tool the host does not provide.

### Workspaces

| Package | Owns | May depend on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `core` | contracts, protocol types, pure reducers/policy, client ports; no Node, Electron or Vue | none |
| `client/backend` | `daemon`, provider drivers, MCP, persistence, git/files, automations, work providers | `core` |
| `client/vue` | reusable product shell, receives a typed `AppClient` at bootstrap | `core` |
| `client/electron` | desktop host composition root | `core`, `vue`; start a built `daemon` artifact, never import backend sources |
| `mobile` | native mobile shells, companion engine, and shared Vue transcript | `core`, `vue`; no Electron, provider process or backend filesystem authority |

Cross-package imports use package names, never deep relative paths. `core` stays
runtime-thin so every client shares one contract without inheriting file authority.

Repository icons and run profiles belong to the owning daemon's private

folders use canonical file URLs. Command working directories resolve against the
selected worktree rather than the primary checkout.
Explicit imports read script and target names from confined package,
Make and Just files without evaluating recipes or copying their bodies. Discovery
does not save or execute actions. The daemon admits
only a saved profile whose command and resolved directory match the user's reviewed
target; directory containment includes real paths and symlinks. Profiles have no
environment field and never copy environment files. Output and run history are
bounded and volatile; inherited credential values are redacted from output returned

The run-profile service owns each command process group through completion, stop,

use the existing agent-location routing; local loopback previews use the existing

Native sidebar organization and idle-sort preferences belong to a host/team pair.
The engine projects activity groups and their order; native clients render those

Recent mobile provider replicas are retained in memory independently of the connection.

## In-app Browser

A desktop preview surface in the tabbed right workspace. The renderer hosts a
sandboxed `<webview>` with one persistent browser partition shared by all agents.
Electron main validates the guest and owns navigation and annotation policy. The renderer never
receives the guest's `WebContents`, cookies or page-scripting access, and
annotations arrive as structured metadata the renderer batches into one prompt.
Browser guest developer tools are independent of the main application renderer's
release-mode DevTools restriction.
Open browser tabs retain their browser identity and latest URL in the per-client
workspace store. Restoring a tab navigates through the normal host browser API;
page contents, navigation history and live guest handles remain ephemeral.
Named web bookmarks belong to the owning client's presentation preferences,
independent of agents and tabs. Stored URLs are normalized HTTP/HTTPS addresses
without embedded credentials; opening one uses the normal host navigation policy.
The settings store retains their client identity separately from shared defaults.
The MCP `browser-open` tool reaches the same surface
through `client/browser/open`; inactive agent workspaces stay mounted but hidden
so browser tools keep working without changing the user's selection.

Browser extensions share that persistent partition. Visualization guests use
separate, temporary per-agent partitions. Clearing browsing data resets website
storage, cookies, cache and open-page history across agents while preserving
extension storage and grants.
Electron owns extension loading, vendor windows, tab registration and the
app-authored Chrome API adapter; extension documents remain sandboxed and ordinary
websites receive no adapter transport. The adapter derives identity from the
calling extension context and enforces optional grants for its own APIs.
Browser subframe redirects to loaded extensions retain Chromium's resource access
checks; the host's top-level URL policy must not cancel dynamic extension resource
redirects. Visualization guests retain their navigation restrictions. Optional
Chromium permissions that Electron cannot grant and revoke are rejected. Native
desktop connections require a current `nativeMessaging` grant and a host listed
for that extension. `daemon` validates the installed host registration, executable
and allowed extension origin; Electron owns the framed native process connection.
Revocation, context teardown and extension unload close those connections. Native
payloads and host stderr are never logged.

`daemon` owns the supported extension allowlist, official CRX3 downloads,
signature and identity verification, package files and per-client grants.
Verified packages are reused locally while account data stays in the shared
Electron partition. The explicit Install action authorizes initial permissions;
updates and runtime requests require consent for additional permissions. Failed
downloads or verification preserve the installed package. Compatibility is not
gated by a tested-version catalog. The passive Bitwarden storage relay belongs to
the extension lifecycle and closes on unload. Explicit removal uses an app-owned
same-identity cleanup context before deleting the extension's scoped storage.

## Interactive planning

Provider-native Markdown proposals own plan review identity and approval. Korus adds
section and selected-text comments and decorates flat Markdown checkbox lists as
multiple choices and `( )` / `(x)` lists as single choices. Other code examples, nested
lists and mixed lists retain normal Markdown rendering. Authored HTML remains
escaped by the shared Markdown renderer. Model-selected defaults are proposals.
Editing a choice includes the selected answers in feedback; resetting the group
removes that feedback. Saved choices survive reloads. Revise and Approve submit
directly after pending edits are saved.

Fenced Mermaid diagrams stay in the native proposal Markdown and render through
the shared read-only Visualize renderer. Whole-diagram comments use the existing
review draft and retain source context for the agent. Plans do not create a
Visualize session or editable canvas state.

The owning host's Workflows setting enables interactive plans by default. Enabled
Plan-mode turns receive hidden Markdown choice and diagram guidance; disabling it leaves
ordinary Markdown and native review actions without choice controls.

Draft feedback belongs to the agent, conversation and native review ID. The owning
host persists it with optimistic versions through the existing review response
contract. Saving does not start a turn. Revise explicitly sends feedback in a
Plan-mode turn, with selected answers and comments inside hidden context; Approve
uses the native implementation authorization path. Persisted delivery intent
prevents automatic retry after an uncertain delivery. New proposals start unanswered and retain prior
feedback in bounded review history.

The Vue editor is keyed by owner and review identity. Its draft and serial saves
survive snapshot updates without replacing document or footer elements. Stale
responses cannot target another review. Saved structured plans migrate to Markdown
and retain their feedback; migration grants approval authority only when the saved
plan matches an existing native review.

## Theming

Components never import fixed colors. Themes are semantic tokens written as CSS
custom properties on the document root; syntax and diff highlighting use the same
theme source. See [frontend.md](frontend.md).

# Backend Architecture

`daemon` is the Korus product backend: a separate Node process that orchestrates
Codex app-server, Claude Code, Antigravity ACP, the Korus MCP server, git, files,
automations, work integrations and persistent state behind one app-owned protocol. It is not a
replacement for Codex app-server. Ownership rules live in
[architecture.md](architecture.md); message contracts in [protocol.md](protocol.md).

The executable is `korusd` (`product.daemonName`). Source filenames, RPC methods,
log and socket paths, npm scripts and launchd labels stay brand-neutral.

## Design Rules

- Routers validate and route; focused services own stateful workflow (retries,
  timers, persistence callbacks, cleanup). Do not grow a request switch into the
  owner of the workflow it exposes.
- Transport-specific clients own only process or socket lifecycle. One shared
  session implementation owns JSON-RPC framing, pending requests, timeouts and
  server callbacks; never copy lifecycle logic into a second transport.
- Provider setup follows the same split: `ProviderLifecycle` adapters own
  executable detection, home preparation and resource sharing;
  `ProviderSetup` owns locking, serialization, persistence and driver replacement.
  Authentication enters through the optional `AgentBackendDriver.authenticate`
  capability; the server caches the app-owned result and never interprets
  credentials or probes provider CLIs itself.
- Provider updates are backend-owned, per installation and host. Version checks
  never install software; explicit consent is tied to a checked installation and
  target version. Waiting upgrades are process-local and cancellable. The runtime
  scheduler starts them only when the provider is idle; admission is blocked while
  its processes are stopped, updated and replaced. Conversation identities remain
  intact. The original installation method/channel is preserved; unknown or
  unsupported installations use official instructions. No provider is installed
  automatically and no app restart is scheduled. Preferences and queued upgrades
  must not be mistaken for permission to interrupt running work.
- Provider detection and launches share `core/runtime-discovery`: the owning
  host's login-shell PATH precedes inherited and fallback directories. Shell PATH
  output is framed so startup messages cannot corrupt executable selection;
  unavailable shells fall back to inherited PATH. Launches resolve the executable
  and child environment together, preserving explicit executable overrides.
  The desktop's private Node is only a child-PATH fallback. npm ownership checks
  and upgrades run the selected npm CLI with its adjacent Node, never whichever
  Node an app-private PATH happens to select.
- Domain modules never self-register global timers. A runtime scheduler runs
  registered tasks (automation scans, PR monitoring) without overlap.
- Queued prompt delivery removes an item only after backend acceptance; transport
  failure keeps the FIFO head and retries with bounded backoff, without duplicate
  user messages.
- Agent creation (protocol, MCP delegation, independent review) goes through one
  `AgentCreationService`; callers only adapt their input.
- Short text utilities use `driver/text/generate` with the initiating agent's
  provider, prompt, optional instructions and output schema. Callers declare task
  complexity instead of provider model IDs; omission retains the simple tier.
  `utilityTextModel` resolves the tier from that provider's native catalog. A
  missing model is an error; utilities never switch providers, send a conversation
  prompt or change the agent's selected model. Provider hosts own isolated
  generation and cleanup. Cancellable utilities carry request IDs across RPC;
  their owning host maps those IDs to local abort signals. Cancellation targets
  the isolated provider conversation and acknowledges its settlement, independently
  of the agent's main conversation. Diff visualization sets `timeoutMs: null`
  across utility RPC and provider generation to wait until completion or cancellation.
  A separate tools flag opts inspection utilities
  into read-only workspace inspection; omission disables workspace-tool access. This
  policy does not control provider-configured tools unrelated to the workspace.
  Diff visualization supplies the agent's working folder and selected Git scope,
  including section filters. The model retrieves focused evidence through tools;
  patch contents are not embedded in its prompt. Native shapes own their component
  and review metadata; navigation stays limited to files and line ranges present
  in the selected comparison. Role icons resolve to app-owned assets in the
  renderer; fetched marks are embedded as bounded image payloads. The renderer sanitizes
  SVG and retains each saved diagram's image bytes without an external registry.
  The bundled `korus-stack-diagram` skill owns the shared architecture-diagram
  guidance. Visualize loads it through `read-skill`; Polished Diff Viz injects the
  same skill text into its utility request. Caller-specific output and evidence
  contracts stay separate from that visual guidance. Composition targets are
  advisory: usable drawings survive extra components, groups, connections and
  longer labels. Optional review metadata is recovered independently; unsupported
  annotations and out-of-scope links are omitted, and dangling bindings become
  standalone geometry. Rendering and safety constraints still reject unusable
  or unsafe content.
  Polished Viz attaches an app-owned PNG composition reference from the runtime
  assets root. Forge ships it outside `app.asar`; standalone daemon staging and
  SSH installation carry the same file beside the daemon. Utility image inputs
  are host-resolved absolute paths, validated as bounded image attachments before
  provider dispatch, and do not enable workspace tools.
- Repository acquisition and branch-to-agent setup share daemon-owned modules
  across desktop and companion adapters. Access adapters may revalidate a grant
  before each write, but do not duplicate checkout selection or clone-reuse rules.
  Close previews come from the daemon; review availability, reviewer defaults and
  quota eligibility use shared product policy. Mutation handlers revalidate their
  conditions before provider or filesystem side effects.
- Optional operator requirements load from `$APP_HOME/requirements.json` before
  services start, separately from app-written settings. Invalid requirements stop
  startup. Model catalog filtering and provider availability belong to the owning
  daemon; clients consume the filtered results. See
  [host requirements](agent-provider-selection.md#host-requirements).

## Antigravity

`client/backend/src/antigravity` owns installation and discovery of the ACP
runtime/harness, OAuth observations, and the provider replica. The agy CLI is not
the execution path. OAuth renewal stays native, background checks suppress login UI,
and child environments sanitize Google credentials/projects with isolated
`GEMINI_HOME` and temporary storage. Home routing is not a filesystem sandbox.
An explicit installation request downloads a pinned Google-hosted archive into
private temporary storage. Size and SHA-256 checks precede bounded extraction of
regular executable files; an ACP handshake in a disposable home verifies the
qualified runtime before atomic activation. Installation never authenticates,
and runtime binaries remain outside app release resources. Provider setup
serializes installation with home changes and detection refreshes. Discovery
accepts the managed pair, paired executables on PATH, explicit runtime/harness
environment paths, or an existing versioned runtime directory.

Each agent owns a process/session with serialized prompts and bounded cancellation.
Cold replay validates session identity and rebuilds atomically: replay tool IDs
differ and later updates may reverse tool status. Unknown timestamps stay absent;
the private prompt journal preserves presentation metadata, never a second transcript.
Session MCP identity/review scope travels in bridge child environments under
`product.mcpServerName`, never shared configuration. Auxiliary generation uses a
separate session with MCP, built-ins and client filesystem requests disabled.

Native catalogs remain authoritative; Korus never impersonates an allowlisted
editor to expose third-party models. Native plan artifacts feed app-owned review,
with implementation in a separate accepted turn. [The plan](../plans/antigravity.md)
records transport evidence, model restrictions, attachment support and unsupported
capabilities.

### Request pricing evidence

Antigravity executions retain turn status and timing with unknown model and token
consumption. Their request coverage is partial with
`acp-request-evidence-unavailable`; analytics includes each execution in the unknown
request count and returns unavailable USD rather than zero. Context notifications,
selected model settings, permission modes and cumulative session costs cannot
establish individual API charges. No underlying provider is inferred from the
Antigravity provider name or the catalog's display names.

The qualified Google-hosted ACP 1.3.0 executable implements the v1-shaped wire
contract while reporting protocol 2. Its bundled Python adapter is the evidence
boundary; the public CLI, Python SDK and Gemini Interactions API are different
interfaces. The [pinned public registry](https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/registry/blob/dc55a34900fdd60e5e97c1cbd7825c5a1df673fc/antigravity-acp/agent.json)
identifies the distribution. [Fixture provenance](../client/backend/src/antigravity/__tests__/fixtures/usage-capability.json)
records archive/executable hashes and source locations. These are source-derived
wire fixtures with synthetic numbers and identities, not a live billing capture.

| Required evidence | Public ACP surface | Pricing consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billable request identity and timestamp | Session ID and JSON-RPC prompt correlation; no identity or timestamp for each underlying model call | Request count remains unknown; a prompt can contain several calls/retries |
| Actual model and underlying API provider | `models.currentModelId`, `availableModels` and model config options describe selection | No served-model assertion, exact API model mapping or provider attribution; Google, Anthropic and OpenAI routes remain unpriced |
| Input/output/cache-read/cache-write counts and inclusion semantics | `server.py::_maybe_send_usage_update` emits only `used` and `size`; `_extract_tokens_used` collapses categories | Context occupancy never becomes measured consumption |
| Cache-write lifetimes | No buckets in emitted updates or the optional schema-level `Usage` | No lifetime assumptions or fabricated zero writes |
| Pricing context | `used` is derived from main-trajectory cumulative deltas, includes output/thinking and caches; `size` uses the selected model's context limit | Neither supplies per-request pricing input; subagent context is excluded and updates can coalesce |
| Served tier/mode | Session mode config describes permissions; no served billing tier/mode in output | No standard-tier default or requested-as-served substitution |
| Finality and completeness | `prompt` returns `PromptResponse(stop_reason=...)` without usage, including cancellation; schema supports optional turn totals but the adapter does not populate them | Completed, failed and interrupted turns retain unavailable coverage |

The [ACP usage contract](https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/v1/prompt-turn#session-usage-updates)
defines `used`/`size` as context utilization and optional `cost` as cumulative
session cost. The shipped schema also defines optional cumulative token categories
on `PromptResponse.usage`. Schema availability does not prove runtime emission or
request boundaries. Regression fixtures exercise those optional fields separately
as negative controls: neither turns into request-aware USD.

To repeat the source check without authentication, use the qualified archive's
`agy_acp_server.par` as the argument below. It reads only the shipped public adapter
and schema, validates stored ZIP-entry checksums, and prints the relevant ranges;
it does not execute the runtime or access a provider endpoint.

```bash
python3 - /path/to/agy_acp_server.par <<'PY'
import hashlib, pathlib, struct, sys, zlib
data = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]).read_bytes()
print('executable sha256:', hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest())
root = 'google3/cloud/developer_experience/antigravity_extensions/acp_server/'
ranges = {
    root + 'server.py': [(1473, 1528), (5283, 5318), (5850, 5941)],
    root + 'config_options.py': [(49, 103)],
    'google3/third_party/py/acp/schema.py': [(1397, 1444), (1697, 1720), (3846, 3880)],
}
found, offset = set(), 0
while (offset := data.find(b'PK\x03\x04', offset)) >= 0:
    header = struct.unpack_from('<IHHHHHIIIHH', data, offset)
    method, checksum, size, name_len, extra_len = header[3], header[6], header[7], header[9], header[10]
    name = data[offset + 30:offset + 30 + name_len].decode('utf-8', errors='replace')
    start = offset + 30 + name_len + extra_len
    if name in ranges and method == 0:
        source = data[start:start + size]
        assert zlib.crc32(source) == checksum
        print(name, hashlib.sha256(source).hexdigest())
        lines = source.decode().splitlines()
        for first, last in ranges[name]:
            for n in range(first, last + 1): print(f'{n}: {lines[n - 1]}')
        found.add(name)
    offset += 4
assert found == set(ranges), 'Required public sources missing; requalify the runtime.'
PY
```

The adapter-to-SQLite-to-`usage/get` workflow is repeatable with
