## Local desktop replacement

Local macOS desktop replacement is owned by the
[`korus-desktop-update` skill](../.agents/skills/korus-desktop-update/SKILL.md) and
its bundled updater. It stages a signed, notarized build or a copy of the installed
app, then uses independent one-shot installer and recovery LaunchAgents. The
installer retains the previous bundle and preserves pairing; startup verification
checks the new desktop and its owned backend before declaring success. Private
transaction logs and profile backups stay in the application home, outside the
source checkout. Provider history is retained in place during activation and
recovery.

## Transports

The protocol is transport-neutral JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line.

| Transport | Use |
| --- | --- |
| stdio (`korusd --stdio`) | bundled local backend; same framing SSH uses |
| Unix socket (`korusd serve`, `APP_HOME/daemon.sock`) | optional always-on single-host daemon |
| SSH stdio | remote locations: noninteractive SSH with keepalives, an app-private Node runtime, and a version-checked socket bridge or one-shot backend |

- Electron's default `APP_BACKEND_MODE=auto` connects to a running local daemon,
  else starts the bundled stdio process. On reconnect it retries the same
  transport with bounded backoff and **never** falls back to a fresh bundled
  daemon after an established connection drops: that would fork authoritative
  state.
- `connect` checks the running socket owner's version before bridging SSH stdio.
  Only an unavailable socket permits a one-shot stdio backend; an incompatible
  live owner requires restarting its service and never permits a second state
  writer. Setup never installs or restarts a persistent remote service.
- No unauthenticated LAN server. Keep Unix sockets in a user-private `APP_HOME`;
  bind any HTTP transport (including the MCP server) to loopback. Add per-user
  tokens before named pipes, cross-user access or any network transport. TCP or
  WebSocket remote control needs its own authenticated design first.
- `stdout` is reserved for JSON-RPC in stdio mode; diagnostics go to stderr and
  `$APP_HOME/logs/daemon.log` (structured JSONL, size-rotated). Redact prompts,
  tokens, OAuth codes, command secrets and file contents from logs.
- `CODEX_APP_SDK_TRACE_CONVERSATION_LOAD=1` enables conversation-load timings

hoices are imported before retiring the old file. Each off-to-on transition sets
`enabledAt`; repeated enable calls and restarts preserve it. Automatic reports
start with the next full UTC hour. The partial hour and time while sharing was off

Only explicit desktop operations return the credential-free sharing choice. The
desktop bridge accepts an action or reporting day, never an identity override.
The conversation-top notice uses the backend consent authority. Its one-minute
foreground timer starts only when the notice is eligible, pauses while hidden or
unfocused, and retains its elapsed time across pane changes in the renderer session.
Timeout persists the enabled setting through the same desktop operation as an
explicit enable, while retaining the notice for the rest of that session until

The consent owner delegates transitions to `TelemetryDeliveryPort`; it does not
send, schedule or manage a queue. One backend `TelemetryUploadService` per local
installation runtime owns sealing, the private durable queue, telemetry HTTP,
acknowledgements and cancellation. RuntimeScheduler checks delivery each minute.
Each installation uploads at the UTC minute given by its UUID modulo 60, once
per hour; startup respects the same slot. The stable slot spreads clients across
the hour independently of local timezone and restarts. It discovers reporting
hours from the local ledger, including
all unsent retained history inside the current sharing window. Electron also signals observed
open/focus/resume activity, and scheduled uploads confirm foreground presence so
an active hour without turns can report empty usage. Remote ledgers and mobile
companions cannot supply local reporting data; an idle daemon cannot invent empty
activity hours.

Delivery state is bound to the installation UUID. It retains the local ledger's
year of hourly buckets, with a 10,000-bucket bound. Frozen pending bodies survive
until delivery finishes; older acknowledgements keep a digest for unchanged-total
comparison. Discovery never reconstructs zero totals from expired source data.
Each flush sends at most ten reports, prioritizing the current hour before older
unsent history. A persisted 30-attempt rolling-hour budget survives restart, and
a 429 pauses the whole backlog. A bounded rotating scan checks acknowledged
buckets for late corrections. Queue writes are atomic and private;
attempts are recorded before transport. Restart preserves frozen bodies and the
six-attempt budget. A lost acknowledgement may cause identical physical retries;
pending reports retry their original bytes. After acknowledgment, a changed
hourly projection replaces that bucket's totals; unchanged projections are skipped.
Corrupt state fails closed rather than reconstructing already-sealed history.

Desktop release builds embed `APP_TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT` from the build environment
as a public fallback in the daemon bundle. A runtime value overrides it; an
explicitly blank runtime value disables it. With neither a runtime value nor a
bundled endpoint, there are no requests, discovery or health checks. Its value is supplied outside Git; HTTPS is required except for explicit
loopback HTTP test receivers. Requests have a ten-second deadline, no credentials
or provider headers, and no redirect following. Network failures, 408, 429 and 5xx
retry with bounded jittered backoff and a capped Retry-After; other responses end
the report. Bodies and response contents never enter logs. App actions do not
wait for telemetry work or present delivery failures.

Disable/reset abort transport and purge activity/pending work
without waiting for ledger reads or acknowledgement. Revocation becomes visible
in memory as soon as requested, including while an earlier consent callback is
pending. Every await before sending is followed by an authority guard;
obsolete work cannot restore a purged report. Preview I/O does not hold the consent
mutation lock, and obsolete preview results are rejected after a transition.
Cancellation is requested even when saving consent fails. Failed user actions
remain visible; durable opt-out still requires a successful local consent write.

The uploader workflow uses temporary real SQLite/private files, fake time and a
loopback HTTP receiver. Repeat with

and exact retry body. This proves local transport behavior, not production
infrastructure privacy. Dependency/AST lint isolates telemetry callers from

Profile preview resolves identity inside the backend. Previews while sharing is
off are hypothetical and cannot enqueue history. An unfinished UTC day is
provisional. For a completed day, a legacy daily report supplied by the delivery owner

The consent no-IP-storage statement requires collector, proxy and upstream

Inclusive input includes cache reads and Claude cache creation. Cached input means
reads only; output already includes reasoning. The input-minus-read remainder
includes writes, so it is not an ordinary-rate fresh-input measurement. Claude's
request observer retains write lifetimes, while execution totals collapse them.
Codex execution cache-write counters, including a schema default of zero, do not
establish inclusion semantics, write lifetime or independently billable request
evidence. The projection uses existing ledger estimate coverage, including its
execution fallbacks; it neither invents request evidence nor reprices usage. Its
omitted cache-write categories prevent exact downstream repricing. Estimated USD
is API-equivalent usage, not billing.

The server-usage workflow compares persisted Claude/Codex measurements against
`client/backend/src/usage/__tests__/fixtures/daily-telemetry.json`, the exact canonical
macOS UTF-8 body without a trailing newline. Other platforms substitute only the
coarse OS value. Repeat with
`npm run test -w @workspace/backend -- usage/__tests__/server-usage.spec.ts`.
It covers UTC bucket attribution, model changes, nulls and
content/local-dimension canaries without an endpoint. Architecture AST lint limits
projection dependencies and rejects direct network/timer operations.

Performance reuses the ledger's additive speed samples: measured output tokens,
active generation milliseconds, summed time to first output, and their turn
counts. Only hourly provider/model/tier sums enter the optional closed performance
object; no per-turn timing or timestamps are exported. Missing samples are
unavailable, not zero. The read API divides the summed output by summed time and
the summed first-output time by its measured-turn count. It never averages
per-install rates. Older reports remain valid without performance fields.
The consent file's second format pauses an older enabled opt-in and presents the
updated explanation before any expanded sharing. Existing declines stay declined.

Hosted ingestion, authentication, reporting and deployment live under `server/`.
See [the hosted server documentation](../server/README.md) for that independent
process boundary. Desktop consent, projection and upload remain daemon-owned.

# Codex Integration

Korus talks to Codex through `codex app-server`, and only from `daemon`. Electron
forwards app-owned RPC and fans events out; the renderer never imports generated
Codex types, spawns Codex or touches `CODEX_HOME`. Read this before changing Codex
conversation state, rendering, actions, history or transport.

## Ownership

The local `codex-app-sdk` owns: executable discovery, generated app-server types,
request/response inference, bidirectional routing, stdio JSONL framing, targeted
conversation operations, snapshots and reducers, optimistic submissions, history
reconciliation, queues, turn mutations and the generic conversation UI
(`CodexConversationPane`). `daemon` is the product adapter: explicit executable
selection, initialization metadata, agent/session policy, approval presets, the
routing envelope (agent, thread, revision) and recovery.

- Generic Codex conversation behavior missing or wrong? Fix it in the SDK and
  consume it. Product policy never goes into the SDK to make a Korus call compile.
- Korus must not add a parallel message store, optimistic row, history or queue
  reducer, or turn-mutation state machine. Korus's own admission queue (whether a
  prompt starts now or waits for the agent) is coordination state, distinct from the
  provider-native queue in the SDK snapshot, and must not be substituted for it.
- Agent text keeps the app-server's optional `commentary`/`final_answer` phase.
  Only app-server reasoning summaries are kept, never raw reasoning content.
- The TypeScript `codex exec` SDK is not an integration boundary; app-server is,
  because the product needs thread list/resume, steering, approval routing, turn
  diffs and server-initiated requests.
- Unimplemented server-initiated request types log `not implemented` and answer a
  JSON-RPC error so app-server never waits forever; unhandled notifications are
  logged. Optional questions do not hold an agent in `awaitingInput`, which is
  reserved for blocking requests and approvals.
- **Readiness is not outcome.** A native thread-idle update releases readiness and
  queued prompts but never fabricates `turn.completed`. Durable task results stay
  provisional until the submitting turn's authoritative terminal event; a late
  terminal event belongs to its original turn and cannot clear a newer active turn.

The SDK's content transport projects embedded image data and large file diffs into content-addressed
references before snapshots and events leave the daemon. Reads use the owning
conversation's current SDK snapshot and bounded chunks. Provider history is untouched;
a weak projection cache does not retain discarded snapshots or create another
transcript store. The SDK also indexes original provider-recorded image outputs by
conversation, turn, call and image identity, and reads their existing history bytes
on demand. This preserves historical screenshots independently of temporary files;
Korus keeps no image archive or history parser. Content reads stay bound to the
owning agent session across asynchronous I/O. Desktop and companion hosts resolve
the same references. File targets carry historical diff references; selecting a file fetches its exact patch in bounded chunks, separately
from the current working-tree source.

The shared renderer loads media and attachment previews near the chat viewport,
with two concurrent reads and placeholders sized from intrinsic image dimensions.
The SDK transport carries optional width and height from bounded header probes;
older images retain their decoded ratio for subsequent cache eviction. Compressed originals and rendered thumbnails share a 64 MiB cache on mobile and
desktop. Offscreen decoded previews are released while downloaded originals stay
cached with their thumbnails, so returning reuses previews without another host read. Inline
thumbnails match their rendered size; opening, copying and downloading use original
bytes. Cached originals are evicted by recency when the cache needs room;
oversized or failed previews remain explicitly retryable. Independent desktop
image tabs own their blob URLs until closed, rather than borrowing an evictable
transcript URL. Provider history, transient decoding, browser caches, and separate
image viewers are outside the transcript preview budget.

## Process And Home

- Executable selection uses the host's discovered PATH, including login-shell and common
  user bin directories for GUI launches, unless an explicit backend
  `codexBinaryPath` override is saved. Without an override, macOS falls back to
  `/Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex-cli/bin/codex` when no CLI is found.
  Detection, launch and version inspection use the same selection policy. Korus
  supplies an explicit command to the SDK to preserve that precedence. Welcome and Settings link to
  official installation documentation; the backend rechecks external installs
  and refreshes a newly available driver without installing or updating a CLI.
- Codex is an external prerequisite; development, packaging and release checks
  do not download or pin the CLI. The app packages its own Node runtime and daemon.
- `CODEX_HOME` follows the persisted provider home, defaulting to the existing CLI
  home for a new setup. Separate setups use `$APP_HOME/codex-home`. Skills
  and plugins sharing, isolation and the roster-reset rules are in
  [architecture.md](architecture.md#provider-homes). Folder-changing actions restart
  `daemon` and need idle chats. Never copy normal Codex thread or auth files.
- Process-wide app-server overrides enable memories and streamed patch events, and
  disable the bundled unified Computer Use plugin (Korus's own MCP tools replace it)
  and the curated GitHub/Linear plugins ([mcp.md](mcp.md)).
- Authentication goes through the SDK account surface: signed-out renders a landing
  gate; browser login (local) or device-code login (SSH host, with its exact login
  ID for cancellation) is SDK-driven. Korus never implements token exchange, copies
  credentials or owns refresh, and raw account types never reach the renderer.
- Shutdown: Electron allows `daemon` 15 s; the SDK closes app-server stdin first so
  provider history flushes before bounded signal escalation.

## Threads And Agents

Codex owns history and thread storage; Korus maps team, agent, folder, display name,
status and `backendSession { kind: "codex", threadId }`. One app-server hosts many
threads, routed by `threadId` and `agentId`.

- A persisted session is resumed with `thread/resume` before the next turn; new
  agents use `thread/start` and set the conversation title to the agent name
  (matching titles are a no-op; renaming the agent renames the conversation).
  Active sessions are SDK-memory-authoritative and are not re-resumed on selection;
  after relaunch `agent/conversation/load` rebinds the persisted reference.
- Archive/reconcile/resume rules are in
  [architecture.md](architecture.md#backend-seam). Resume searches active and
  archived catalogs with the agent folder as exact `cwd`; `storageState` marks
  archived rows; a failed load rearchives the target and restores the current runtime.
- Fork (agent- or turn-level) calls the SDK conversation handle's `fork()` /
  `forkTurn()`; raw fork types stay out of product contracts. It requires an idle
  agent with an existing conversation and creates a new selected agent below the
  source.
- Worktree delegation forks through the same SDK handle with the worker's cwd,
  model, effort, service tier, permissions and extension context. A running
  source forks at its last completed turn; without a completed boundary it
  falls back to a fresh handoff. Worker instructions explicitly bind the current
  identity and folder so inherited parent assignments cannot redirect execution.
- **Compress Session is session rollover, not Codex compaction.** For an idle agent:
  ask the SDK conversation for a bounded handoff with a temporary fast model/effort
  override, wait for that exact turn, create a replacement conversation in the same
  folder with the original settings, send the handoff inside a real initial prompt
  (the SDK strips its `<context>` block from the visible message), and only then
  archive the old thread and update the persisted reference. The handoff turn's
  settings and events are internal and must not change persisted defaults. If
  creation or archiving fails the agent keeps its old thread. Never build a parallel
  handoff transcript or synthetic message.
- Continue on an interrupted turn is a dedicated action that starts a turn with empty
  input after confirming the latest turn is interrupted; it never submits the text
  "continue".
- Review: independent or current-thread rules are in
  [architecture.md](architecture.md#code-review). Review rounds replace the normal
  MCP URL with the review-session URL ([mcp.md](mcp.md)). `review/start` uses inline
  delivery and a different returned review thread ID is a protocol error rather than
  a session move; the `exitedReviewMode` body renders as assistant text.
- Personalization edits `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`) in each provider's configured
  home on the owning host; changes apply when sessions start or resume, never as a
  message in an active turn. Mission contracts and developer instructions are
  applied at session configuration, never injected as user messages.
- Image generation requested by another engine is a Korus-owned internal Luna job.
  It uses existing SDK conversation creation, events and generated media; no
  protocol parsing or transcript reduction belongs in the bridge. The conversation
  is never bound to a roster agent and is deleted after the job. Model selection
  comes from the current catalog and never falls back to a different model family.

Historical conversation loading requests SDK summaries independently of turn paging.
Completed turns retain their prompt and final answer; expanding Working details asks
the owning SDK handle for that turn and receives normal replica updates. Desktop,
shared conversations and native mobile forward the same operation; they do not
reconstruct omitted messages or keep a second history cache. Live turns remain full,
and exhaustive reads for handoffs and other backend consumers use SDK `readHistory`.

## Settings And Policy

- **Approval presets** are app-owned shortcuts over thread settings; the renderer
  sees only the preset ID and `daemon` maps it to `approvalPolicy`,
  `approvalsReviewer` and sandbox for `thread/start|resume` and live updates. Do not
  reuse them for Claude's permission modes. Before applying one, `daemon` reads
  `configRequirements/read`: a disallowed preset clamps to the best compatible
  (`approve-for-me`, `ask-for-approval`, `full-access`), and if none fits `daemon`
  omits approval/sandbox overrides and lets app-server use its effective
  configuration rather than sending a known-invalid request. The generated
  `SandboxPolicy` shape is returned directly.
- **Models and effort** come from `model/list`, adapted to `BackendModelOption[]`.
  Korus prefers 6.1 Sol with High effort when advertised by the catalog and uses
  that combination for new conversations without an explicit selection.
  An explicit picker choice is saved immediately in
  `backendDefaults` as user-selected, restored before publishing loaded conversations,
  and cannot be replaced by later thread events; each
  prompt captures model, effort and service tier in its options, including queued
  ones. The service tier (Fast mode) is emitted with thread settings, including an
  explicit `null`, so a stale toggle never survives an agent switch or reload.
- **Skills** are folder-scoped (`skills/list` per agent `cwd`), adapted to
  `BackendSkillSummary[]`. Picker selection records the canonical target and frozen
  display label in authored prompt parts. The SDK sends explicit skill and mention
  inputs; typed or pasted `$skill` and `@name` text carries no selected identity.
  `skills/changed` becomes `skills.changed` and invalidates folder-keyed caches.
- **Composer commands:** `@` files, `$` skills, `/` commands then skills. `/compact`
  (bare, menu action or Command-K) opens Compress Session; `/compact <text>` is an
  ordinary prompt. Bare `/review` opens Korus's review setup without a visible turn
  (same for Claude); `/review <text>` calls `review/start`. `/plan` toggles composer
  Plan mode (bare, or with a prompt submitted as `planMode: true`). `/goal` mutates
  thread metadata without a turn (`/goal clear` works while busy;
  pause/resume are unsupported).
- **Plan mode** uses `turn/start.collaborationMode`. It must be sent even without a
  selected model (`daemon` omits `settings.model`, uses the Plan preset's `medium`
  effort and `developer_instructions: null`). Because Codex persists the mode,
  leaving Plan mode must send `mode: "default"`; omitting it keeps the thread in
  Plan. Korus mode selections first await the SDK's persistent conversation
  setting, then submit the prompt. This keeps the composer and restored settings
  aligned with execution; the SDK's send option alone overrides only one turn.
  Composer mode also follows the SDK snapshot and settings events so transport
  recovery does not depend on a transient mode notification. Snapshots with an
  unchanged mode preserve an unsent local mode selection.
- **Plans:** `turn/plan/updated` is the structured execution plan (complete only when
  every step is, finalized as incomplete/interrupted/failed at `turn/completed`).
  `item/plan/delta` drafts a proposed plan (experimental); the completed `plan` item
  is authoritative and overwrites the draft. Raw response messages are diagnostic
  only, and plan Markdown never renders as assistant text. Plan preview actions:
  Confirm exits Plan mode and sends `implement the plan`; Cancel exits and sends
  nothing; Comment keeps Plan mode and sends the inline comments as a refinement.
- **Goals** are durable thread metadata; the goal shelf and pending-goal pill are SDK
  UI. `thread/goal/*` notifications become app-owned goal events.
- **Usage:** context occupancy is `last.totalTokens / modelContextWindow` (`total` is
  cumulative and can exceed the window; cap displayed numerators).
  `account/rateLimits/updated` is a sparse, account-level update emitted
  opportunistically during streaming, so `daemon` persists the latest value.
  Banked resets use a dedicated, bounded account read through the optional public
  SDK rate-limit surface. Their authoritative decimal count and optional bounded
  details and account credit balances are settings-only responses, never workspace
  snapshots or telemetry. Opaque credit IDs stay in the driver; temporary
  account-bound references identify confirmed redemption selections. Uncertain
  attempts retain their idempotency key, including renderer reloads. Account
  changes invalidate selections and pending operations. Quota notifications do
  not trigger banked-reset reads; confirmed outcomes trigger a fresh account read.
- **Cost estimates:** analytics prices the retained execution model and token counters
  using historical OpenAI rates. Cached reads receive their own rate and reasoning
  already included in output is not charged again. Missing tiers use normal pricing;
  aggregate estimates do not apply long-context premiums. Updates replace the same
  execution estimate, including after replay and restart. Request observations, when
  present, supersede the execution estimate instead of being charged twice.
  The SDK's optional `executionUsage.requestUsage` projection describes independent
  request telemetry; its absence or unavailable result does not prevent an aggregate
  estimate. Execution estimates have a separate count and never invent request IDs.
  Missing model, token counts or model rates still leave cost unavailable. Korus
  does not parse raw notifications or conversation logs for pricing.
- **Compaction:** the SDK converts the `contextCompaction` item (and the deprecated
  `thread/compacted`) into provider events; Korus transports them and never
  synthesizes its own lifecycle.

## Server Requests

`daemon` stores each pending request, emits an app-owned prompt event and resolves or
rejects the server request when the client answers. MCP approval maps to
`confirm_tool` ([mcp.md](mcp.md)). `item/tool/requestUserInput` maps to an `ask_user`
request (stable question IDs, options, multi-select, secret flags); user
cancellation answers an empty map so app-server does not wait. Generated types live
in the SDK; never encode tool calls as id8-style `<tool>` text tags.

## Tests

Integration tests use a typed fake Codex SDK surface with the real Korus driver,
adapter and server; the SDK repository owns app-server transport and
conversation-reducer tests. A real app-server smoke test is opt-in behind an
environment variable. See [testing.md](testing.md).

# Custom MCP Tools

How to add a tool to the `korus` MCP server ([mcp.md](mcp.md) describes the model).
A tool is a product capability, not an MCP schema: `daemon` owns its behavior, the
app-owned protocol carries any client effect, and Vue owns its presentation. Use the
smallest path that works: a pure coordinator query needs no renderer event; a native
desktop action does.

```text
backend agent -> korus MCP tool -> daemon coordinator/service
              -> optional app-owned event or client request -> renderer / Electron
```

Provider adapters only make the server available; tool semantics stay
provider-neutral.

## Steps

1. Define the domain input and result.
2. Implement it in `AppMcpAgentCoordinator` (agent/team state transitions, effects
   injected as callbacks so it has no renderer or Electron dependency) or in
   `AppMcpService` when it needs the snapshot, a driver, persistence or an app
   event. Shared event payloads go in `core/src/contracts.ts`, durable reductions in
   core, transient visual effects in Vue. Route through Electron only for genuinely
   native capabilities.
3. Register the schema and handler in the module that owns the behavior.
4. Add an app-owned event or client request only if the effect crosses the backend
   boundary.
5. Add tool-row presentation if the generic `Ran …` title is not enough.
6. Cover every boundary crossed (below).

Done means the tool is model-discoverable, its result is bounded and useful, its UI
effect is observable, and live and restored rows render the same meaning.

## Registration

Tool families are self-contained modules resolved per authenticated request;
`client/backend/src/mcp/tools.ts` only composes the modules its providers return. A
contextual family (such as Visualize) is an `AppMcpToolModuleProvider` whose
`resolve` returns a module only for an agent in that context, attached via
`AppMcpServiceOptions.toolModuleProviders`. Never add a family-specific branch to
the composer or to unrelated modules. Provider and module IDs are unique and
composition rejects duplicates. A module can claim a shared workflow capability
(Mission owns proposed actions, so the collaboration `finish_turn` schema omits the
generic proposal flags).

- Descriptions state the operation's contract, scope and essential restraints;
  parameter descriptions explain inputs, not workflows. Multi-step procedures
  belong in bundled skills, reached by a short trigger in the owning tool or
  assignment. Keep identity, authorization and turn-lifecycle essentials in
  `client/backend/src/mcp/agent-prompts.ts`; task prompts supply actual scope, state and
  delivery authority rather than repeating the procedure.
- Caller identity comes from the agent-scoped URL; never add an agent ID to a schema.
- Wrap handlers in `loggedToolResult()`; raise deliberate domain errors with
  `McpToolError` (anything else still becomes an `isError` result).

## Status Has Two Meanings

`set-status` changes the agent (`statusText`, cleared when the turn completes, short
and about current activity), independent of runtime state (`idle`, `working`,
`awaitingInput`, `error`). A tool that changes agent state makes the transition
explicit and emits its app-owned event; never infer state from how a row renders.

A tool-call's `running`/`completed`/`failed` lifecycle is presentation of the
conversation row only and never touches `statusText`. `set-status` and `finish_turn`
are hidden from the conversation (dedicated UI) but remain in the provider
transcript.

## Structured Results And Bounded Data

Return results with `structuredToolResult()` (stable keys such as `success`,
`kind`, `message`). Korus does not persist arbitrary tool input and output, since
provider payloads can contain large output, screenshots, file content or secrets.
`client/backend/src/codex/codex-surface-adapter.ts` projects an **allowlist** of
presentation-safe keys before messages enter state. To surface a new value: use a
small scalar or bounded object, add only that key to the projection, add a
real-shape adapter regression proving it survives live and hydrated history, and
keep large or sensitive siblings out. A denylist is wrong here because a new
provider field would reach durable snapshots before anyone classified it.

## Tool-Row Presentation

`client/vue/src/tool-presentation.ts` (recognized tools, icons), `tool-title-presenter.ts`
(phase-aware titles and targets) and `i18n/messages.ts` (running, completed, failed
strings). A visible tool needs a `TOOL_KEYS` entry, a semantic icon group and all
three lifecycle strings ("Creating / Created / Failed creating worktree
feature/x"). Presenters must tolerate missing fields (older persisted
conversations lack new metadata). Rows are status summaries; raw IDs and payloads
belong in expanded content or logs.

## Client Effects

Transient effects (celebrations, spoken acknowledgments) are requested, never
guaranteed: the result confirms `requested`, not `displayed`.

- `finish_turn` can pick one flag, one finish announcement and one celebration in a
  single call. Flags come from a strict allowlist in core and describe typed thread
  state, not presentation. `announcement.text` is trimmed to 160 characters
  and the phase is implied by the tool.
- Celebration requests are boolean. The daemon randomly chooses a visual effect,
  excluding its previous choice; receiving clients still apply display eligibility.
- Spoken acknowledgments: `daemon` applies persisted enablement and dictated-input
  policy and sends the provider-neutral `client/spokenAnnouncement/queue` request
  with no voice or client assumption. Electron picks the current client's voice,
  rechecks mute, selected-agent and foreground eligibility at playback, cancels
  speech that becomes ineligible, and returns as soon as its single no-overlap queue
  accepts the phrase (it coalesces and rate-limits). Phrase text and suppression
  reasons stay out of the MCP result and the normalized renderer projections.
  Synthesis failure is silent and never fails or delays the task; there is no
  system-voice fallback. A new platform implements the same one-phrase helper
  protocol behind this seam, with no renderer branches or provider-specific tools.

## Tests

One focused test per seam crossed: registration/schema/routing
(`client/backend/src/mcp/__tests__/tools.spec.ts`), domain behavior
(`agent-coordinator.spec.ts`), snapshot mutation, events and client effects
(`service.spec.ts`), bounded projection (`codex-surface-adapter.spec.ts`), durable
reducers (`core/src/__tests__`), titles and icons
(`client/vue/src/__tests__/tool-title-presenter.spec.ts`, `tool-presentation.spec.ts`), and
component or app-state tests for visible effects. Start with the smallest red test.

# Frontend

The renderer is Vue 3 with TypeScript and Element Plus. This is a working guide for
consistent implementation. Feature behavior belongs in tests; process and backend
ownership in [architecture.md](architecture.md). Update this guide only when a
reusable convention or canonical component changes.

## Working Method

1. Inspect the nearest component and its colocated tests.
2. Search `client/vue/src/shared/` and `client/vue/src/components/` by interaction and product
   concept before creating markup or CSS (historical names do not prove a component
   is single-use).
3. Choose the narrowest owner: component, renderer state, composable, view model,
   core policy, SDK, or host capability.
4. Reuse a component only when its contract fits without caller-specific flags. Keep
   one-off composition product-local and promote it after a second real use. When a
   canonical component does not fit, record the mismatch.
5. Verify per [testing.md](testing.md); for visible behavior add one proportional
   runtime, DOM or screenshot check when tooling exists.

Done means ownership is clear, reuse is justified and behavior is specified at its
public seam.

## Visual Direction

`docs/codex.png` is the shell shape: navigation left, conversation center, workspace
artifacts right. The app is a dense operational workspace: quiet, compact,
border-light and stable during loading and streaming; concrete actions, restrained
weight and predictable geometry over decorative cards or explanatory copy.

## Ownership

- **Components:** ephemeral interaction and derived presentation state.
- **Shared Quick Chats:** saved joins appear in their original local team's Quick
  Chat list with a shared origin marker. Pasted invitations and native deep links
  use the same join dialog. The daemon owns credentials and provider replicas;
  Vue receives only a credential-free view. The normal conversation component
  uses a text-only proposal composer and guest-scoped image/content readers.
  Shared rows have no local provider session or workspace authority.
  Their titles preserve the owner's label. Sidebar title disambiguation applies
  only to matching names within the same repository group; other repositories,
  folders and Quick Chats do not affect those titles.
  Invitation form state is independent of background join projections; saved
  preferences finish loading before an incoming invitation is prepared.
  Owner and guest suggestions use the SDK's `composer-drawers` slot and shared
  drawer components, including the queued-prompt layout; the daemon owns
  proposal state and authorship, while the renderer owns the editable owner draft.
- **`client/vue/src/app-state.ts`:** renderer state shared across surfaces, the replica of
  server-authored app state, and the registry of per-agent provider replicas. It
  routes provider frames to the matching provider reducer and never interprets or
  rebuilds transcripts. It delegates catalogs, authorization, unread policy, history
  paging and repository discovery to focused `*-state.ts` modules.
- **Composables:** reusable stateful behavior (async loading, caching, request
  lifecycle, mutations). `AppShell` delegates multi-step workflows (onboarding,
  repository acquisition, work-item routing, per-agent right workspace, annotation) to
  `use-*.ts` composables; shells coordinate and keep only navigation and one-step
  event forwarding.
- **Core** owns cross-client policy and contracts, specified in core tests.
- Sidebar organization is a client-local, per-team preference. Repository and
  Worktree views use the same agent identities; Worktree groups exact Git branch
  names across repositories from backend workspace metadata. Creating agents does
  not change that preference, and detached or non-Git sessions retain their own
  groups. Labels come from persisted team metadata. Opening a group assigns only
  its members to the existing split layout, capped at four in sidebar order; a
  three-agent group keeps the fourth pane empty. Cockpit stays in Activity view.
- **Product components** (`client/vue/src/components/`) represent one product concept with
  typed props and semantic emits. **Shared primitives** (`client/vue/src/shared/`) are
  domain-neutral with isolated tests and never import product components, stores,
  views or backend clients.
- **SDK surfaces** own conversation, composer, message, tool, approval, attachment,
  clipboard and transcription behavior. **Host capabilities** own Electron/web
  differences (dialogs, Browser views, Computer Use, Open In, Dock badges).
- Components consume app-owned contracts, never provider types, Electron globals,
  filesystem APIs or raw backend payloads.

Rules of thumb:

- `App` mounts the shell only after synchronization yields a connected workspace
  snapshot; an empty placeholder or failed read is not evidence of first-run
  onboarding. Later disconnects keep the mounted workspace intact.
- Use `AsyncCatalogCache` for keyed async catalogs (dedupe, invalidation, stale
  rejection, pushed updates) and `shared/use-debounced-save` for autosaved settings
  (immutable snapshots, serialized writes, flush on disposal and before switching
  resources). Commit an async result only while its request identity still matches
  the active selection.
- Name components after product concepts; use typed `defineProps`/`defineEmits`;
  prefer computed presentation state; split a child when it has its own identity,
  state machine, reusable behavior or test seam; keep styles scoped unless a token,
  reset, shell rule or shared primitive is intentionally global; keep wrappers only
  when they add product semantics.
- Use `shared/use-collapsible-pane-resize` for collapsible pane drags. Keep the
  gesture owner mounted when its pane closes so the same drag can reopen it;
  callers own visibility, width constraints and the restored width. Split dividers
  configure the opposite pane on the same gesture rather than adding a second handler.

### Conversation Panes

`CodexConversationPane` from `@codex-app-sdk/vue` is the complete conversation and
composer surface. Extend it through its controller, slots and typed actions; Korus's
wrapper only maps app state and product routing. Codex panes receive the SDK-owned
snapshot and call targeted SDK bridge operations; Claude panes receive the Claude
host's snapshot. A generic Codex interaction defect is an SDK defect. Never add a
global message list or provider-neutral reducer to `app-state.ts`; Korus-only
overlays read the provider frame or an explicit coordination projection.

Mentions are authored parts created by picker selection, with stable targets and
frozen labels. Drafts, saved selections, queues, submissions and mobile transports
preserve those parts; catalogs never reinterpret plain text. The SDK owns editing
and slicing parts, while Korus supplies selected teammate identities to providers.
Provider dispatch uses the SDK's canonical projection while preserving hidden
context: selected skills become Markdown references with their canonical names
and paths, independently of the saved UI labels.

Split layouts hold peer conversation panes, never parent/child agents.
`useSplitWorkspace` owns layout, assignment, focus and split ratios per team,
persisted in client-local storage so devices retain their own workspace preferences.
The grid constrains displayed ratios to keep panes usable at the current window size;
compact screens show one conversation without replacing the saved layout. Controllers and
async actions keep an explicit agent ID (background updates never select a pane); only
the focused conversation handles global composer and interrupt shortcuts; hydration
watches stable conversation identity, not snapshot object identity. One artifact
sidebar follows the selected agent, keeping each agent's tabs separately.

Desktop conversation image previews preserve the native host's attachment
capabilities. Local paths in assistant image Markdown use the daemon file-preview
API with the containing pane's agent identity, so project and remote-host files
are resolved on their owning host. The renderer receives bounded image data URLs;
it does not read the filesystem or treat project paths as attachment capabilities.

Mobile retains immutable conversation images as binary bytes in each platform's
OS-purgeable cache directory. A shared 256 MiB budget evicts the least recently
accessed images across paired hosts; there is no time expiry. Keys include host,
provider and conversation identity. Forgetting a host clears its entries. Mutable
file paths bypass this cache, and missing, corrupt or unavailable entries fall
back to the authorized host reader. Disk caching leaves viewport loading and the
renderer memory budget independent.

The mobile preview pool survives conversation switches within one connected
host and engine instance. Recent previews share the 64 MiB renderer budget and
are evicted before visible images. Disconnecting, changing the paired host, or
restarting the engine disposes the pool and its object URLs.

The native transcript and shared conversation pane must resolve one SDK Vue
instance: host capabilities use module-local injection keys. The mobile bundler
deduplicates SDK modules across workspace installations to preserve that context.

The file explorer uses directory entries from the owning daemon rather than the
composer's bounded file catalog. Directory pages are cached by the explorer's
agent and folder identity; refresh invalidates those pages. Workspace search
runs independently of loaded tree nodes, so an unopened directory remains searchable.

### Surfaces

- **Backlog** (work-provider inbox) and **Cockpit** (all-teams activity workspace) are
  distinct global surfaces. Opening Cockpit must not load Backlog data. Cockpit
  reuses `AgentSidebarActivity` with fixed activity ordering and no creation controls;
  selecting agents or Missions keeps the global scope until a team is selected.
  Projection and sorting live in a focused view model, not `AppShell`.
- `AgentSidebar` routes the saved team organization choice to `AgentSidebarRepo`
  or `AgentSidebarActivity`. Repository layout and styles remain independent of
  activity sections. Both use common base styles and the shared sidebar controller
  for navigation, menus, resizing, and client-local preferences. Cockpit always
  routes to the activity view.
- Activity sidebar grouping and recency belong to `core/src/workspace-sidebar.ts`;
  desktop and mobile own their local view preference, clock and transitions. Native
  activity rows share one identity space across groups so regrouping preserves rows.
- Team-rail dot: red for unread, orange for working, unread wins, never on the
  selected team or while Cockpit is selected. Agent activity is stored apart from
  metadata so startup hydration does not make idle agents look active.
- Duplicate and fork creation insert the new agent immediately after its source
  in the creating client's saved order. Background copies keep the current selection.
- Mission navigation reuses the workspace group, session row and status-dot
  primitives of Quick Chats. Mission surfaces show artifacts for review with comments
  flowing through the conversation; they have no setup or artifact-editing forms.
  Mission-owned workers stay out of the global agent sidebar.
  Conversation selection is remembered per Mission in client-local storage and
  falls back to the Mission lead when the selected worker is unavailable.
  Pane zoom is also remembered per Mission in client-local storage.
  Mission previews reuse workspace surfaces inside a modal instead of consuming
  workspace columns. Agent Markdown requests share one replaceable pending request per Mission.
  Pending requests do not select an agent or alter the workspace layout. Native
  plans retain their separate review lifecycle.
  Mission activity aggregates the lead and repository agents in priority order:
  any agent needs input, unread lead, any agent working, then idle, independently
  of workflow completion. Desktop and mobile use the same aggregation policy.
  Desktop Dock and team-rail unread badges count ordinary conversations and current
  Mission leads; hidden workers retain their unread state within the Mission.

statistics and file lists; optional lockfile contributions let the renderer filter
stats and previews without changing staging, commits or other Git operations.

## Interaction

Git merge and agent worktree deletion share `GitOperationFeedback`. Their operation
lifetime is independent of dialog visibility: backgrounding dismisses the dialog
without cancelling the request, and completion reports through a notification.
Each request retains its original agent and cleanup choices; completion must not
replace a newer dialog or navigation selection.

- **Dialogs:** single-input prompts use `FormDialog` with `compact` and a subtle
  `ClearableTextInput`. Autofocus runs after dialog focus trapping, with optional
  selection of existing values. Compose `FormDialog`/`FormField` (title, optional subtitle, one
  padded body, labels above controls, divided footer, no second gutter). Footer:
  dismiss tertiary, alternatives secondary, at most one primary, ordered left to
  right as tertiary, secondary, primary. Compact pickers use
  the filter as the whole top row, then loading/error/empty/results. Dialogs emit
  domain actions; the parent or composable persists and calls the backend.
  Header controls teleport their dialogs to the document body so split-pane headers
  and resize handles stay below modal overlays. Keep each dialog’s state and actions
  with its originating control.
  Shared dialog styles reset inherited text alignment to left; footer actions stay
  right-aligned. Do not add per-dialog alignment resets.
- **Menus and tabs:** `AppMenu` gives consistent rows, roles and states; add roving
  focus and Arrow/Home/End to `AppMenu` itself while the containing overlay owns
  Escape, closing and focus return. Share one item model between inline and menu
  actions. Use Element Plus teleport/placement for popovers, Element Plus tabs for
  navigation, radio/segmented controls for exclusive form choices; pill tabs keep
  symmetric edge padding.
  Nested menus stay inside their owning overlay's outside-click boundary. Selection
  and Escape dismissal restore trigger focus after the popup closes.
  Exclusive-choice popup menus show the selected option with `CheckIcon` in place
  of its leading icon; other options keep their normal icons. Use radio items
  with `checked` for accessibility and `:show-selection-check="false"` on `AppMenu`
  so the selected row has one leading checkmark, not an additional trailing one.
- **Lists:** `AppDataList` for dense data, focused rows for navigation. Make the
  whole row the primary target with quiet, keyboard-reachable secondary actions;
  hover and focus keep geometry stable; titlebars align to the shared appbar height;
  each pane owns its scroll axes.
- **Forms:** `FormSection` is the card; its body holds either `FormRow`s (label and
  description left, control right: preferences, toggles, single values) or
  `FormField`s in a two- or three-column grid (label above: related fields being
  configured, e.g. Automations). One section may mix both. `density="compact"` tightens
  `FormSection` rows and switches `FormField` to the grid layout; dialogs keep the
  default.

## Styling And Feedback

- Semantic variables for colors and repeated design values; component-specific
  geometry stays local. Derive Element Plus overrides from the same variables and
  scope them to the owning wrapper. Bridge themes into the SDK through documented
  `--codex-*` variables and `data-codex-theme`; never restyle SDK internals.
- App chrome (buttons, menus, headers) is unselectable; conversation and document
  content stays selectable. Native system sans stack, restrained weights.
- Make loading, working, awaiting-input, empty, offline, error and interrupted
  states explicit near what they affect. Drive staged steps from real backend phases;
  timing may smooth completion but must never imply a phase finished early.
- The in-app browser's `<webview>` sits in the workspace DOM so menus and dialogs
  layer over it; never hide the page to expose an overlay.

Native mobile sheets use an opaque, light neutral canvas with white grouped rows
and subtle separators, adapting both surfaces in dark mode. A shared sheet style keeps settings destinations, forms and
footers consistent in light and dark mode. Camera and image content retain their
own contrast treatment; system pickers retain their native controls.
Long-running operations replace their sheet forms with `AppSheetProgress`, using
one centered layout for the operation, context and indeterminate indicator. Progress
uses the medium sheet height; multi-step sheets keep Cancel at the trailing edge
and Back at the leading edge throughout the flow.
Actions and dismissal remain unavailable until the operation resolves; failures
return to the form with its inputs preserved.

## Accessibility And Copy

- Every icon-only control has an accessible name; keep native keyboard behavior,
  visible focus and predictable focus return; one semantic target per action, no
  nested interactives.
- Short, concrete labels. Reusable copy lives in `client/vue/src/i18n/messages.ts` (use
  `vue-i18n` for dynamic labels). Backend and IPC send app-owned error and status
  descriptors that only the rendering client localizes; raw backend, provider, Git
  or shell text stays diagnostic detail.

## Themes

Components never import fixed colors. Themes are `ThemeDefinition`s of semantic
tokens (`--color-*`, `--diff-*`) applied as CSS custom properties on the document
root; syntax and diff highlighting share the theme source. VS Code theme import is a
desired direction, not a requirement.

## Private Usage Console

`server/frontend/src` is a standalone Vue entry point for aggregate telemetry.
It imports browser-safe contracts and chart policy from core, with no dependency
on client code. The console owns its controls, assets and semantic theme.
Dependency lint enforces that boundary.

Desktop and console analytics use Chart.js through vue-chartjs. Core owns the
browser-neutral chart configuration, numeric bounds, scales and provider/model
palette; each renderer supplies its own aggregate adapter, theme tokens and
accessible tooltips. Quantities use stacked areas or bars. Rates and ratios use
unfilled lines with points, preserving gaps for missing measurements. Keyboard
inspection supports Left/Right and Home/End. Exact PostgreSQL values remain in
console tooltips even when their magnitude exceeds safe canvas coordinates.

Vue Router history routes separate login and the report pages. Authentication
resolves before protected pages render, including on reload and direct links.
Date and usage-filter state stays in the mounted
console across page changes; browser history and direct report links select the
report independently of those filters. Models leads with ranked usage and offers
stacked bars or lines over time. Performance compares model-day rates using the
same model/tier identities, with five most-used variants selected initially.

Sign-in, sign-out and expired-session recovery share the console identity.
Reporting data and credentials are not kept in browser storage.

The private proxy owns authentication. Browser code performs only same-origin
aggregate reads, keeps no credentials or metrics in storage, discards stale filter
responses and clears displayed data during reload or access failure. Activity
cards and series stay global; usage filters affect usage summaries and model rows.

## Editable Visualize Canvases

Visualize imports Mermaid, SVG and image input into an Excalidraw canvas (read-only
with pan by default; Edit unlocks). After import `Visualization.canvas` is
authoritative: **never regenerate Mermaid over an edited canvas**. Mermaid imports as
native shapes; SVG, generated images and converter fallbacks are rasterized sanitized
content, not editable vectors. `ExcalidrawCanvas.vue` owns save scheduling and
selection persistence; `excalidraw-editor.ts` isolates the React SDK, browser-only
Mermaid import, sanitization, exports and cleanup. The canvas has no composer: the
normal conversation handles change requests and the agent reads the saved selection
through its canvas tools.

Stack diagrams use the editor's native Nunito and Cascadia Code families, keeping
saved scenes compatible with Excalidraw. Names and group headings use Nunito;
short technical subtitles use smaller muted Cascadia text. Both renderer hosts
ship the editor's font resources through the shared Excalidraw asset plugin.
Native loading and PNG/SVG exports use the editor's font lifecycle, with fonts
embedded in standalone SVGs. Retained custom font IDs normalize to the native
pairing when imported. Relationship labels bind to their arrows and inherit the
arrow color; retained standalone Diff Viz labels use their nearest connection.

Elements, assets, selection, revision and a bounded PNG preview persist through the
daemon's save method, with no hosted editor or browser database. Saves carry the
Visualize session ID and expected revision (a final save may finish after the pane
closes); conflicting revisions are rejected without replacing local edits. Agent
batches are one undo unit; editor history is local and resets on remount. Git
workspace diagrams belong to the primary worktree's repository identity, so linked
worktree agents share the library, while pane visibility, suggestions, selection and
tool authorization stay conversation-scoped.

## Design Documents

The composer menu, command palette and `/design` share the Design opener.
Agents may offer an exploration, but `open-design` requires an explicit user request
or confirmation. It opens the caller’s saved workspace without submitting a new
provider turn; the caller continues with the Design tools. Exploration grants no
implementation authority.

Design keeps authored HTML node trees, stable IDs, embedded CSS and data-image assets
in daemon-owned documents. User and agent edits share serialized, revision-checked
operations. Text changes target leaves; structural operations preserve unrelated
nodes. Full-document replacement is unavailable after creation. Undo and redo are
client-owned: the panel stacks the previous content of every new revision it sees, its own or the agent's, in one
localStorage entry per agent, and restores it through a user-only `replace` request at the expected revision. The daemon
never stores or sends that history. Autosaves of one field made within five seconds of each other are one undo step.
It survives a restart only while the saved revision still matches the design, and
it is removed with its agent. Named checkpoints recover saved content across restarts while revisions remain monotonic.
Saved Design changes publish only the owning agent's workspace state; they never
replace the client roster containing projected remote agents. Desktop reference
attachments pass through the native attachment registry before provider dispatch.

Artboard operations share the same atomic edit batches. Duplication remaps authored
IDs, CSS selectors and interaction targets; it leaves comments on their original
targets. Each artboard can own its stylesheet, with the document stylesheet as a
legacy fallback. Design notes are saved content, distinct
from the editor's current selection. Undo/redo retain both document content and
artboard operations while the stored revision still matches.

Artboard coordinates belong to saved content; viewport pan and zoom do not.
Artboards without explicit coordinates retain their derived horizontal positions.
Moving an artboard never rewrites the layout inside it.
The canvas reserves display-only gutters for readable captions between stacked
screens. Those gutters stay fixed during a drag and never change saved coordinates.

Layer moves preserve stable identity and comments within their artboard; copies get
new identities and remapped CSS selectors and internal targets. Removing a subtree
also removes its comments and clears links to its removed targets. Element style
and attribute patches use null to remove an authored override. Structural edits
cannot move artboard roots, create cycles, or insert children into text/void nodes.

The inspector serializes debounced saves and retains edits typed during a pending
save. Revision checks reject stale drafts without replacing either version. Pane state and selection belong to
the agent. A missing provider reference does not discard the design; opening the
pane can attach its saved document to the agent's current conversation.

The shared canvas gives every artboard its own opaque-origin frame at a common
zoom. Canvas navigation and inspector visibility are local presentation state;
they do not mutate authored content. An active gesture freezes rendered content
until it finishes, while newer authoritative revisions continue arriving. A stale
gesture stays available for explicit retry or discard against the latest document.

Artboards render at an opaque origin in a sandboxed iframe with a restrictive CSP.
The gesture bridge checks source, token and stable node identity; it exposes no app
capabilities. Play follows declared artboard navigation and Back actions, alongside
local visibility/scroll actions and native controls. Screen history and live form
state are presentation state, separate from saved selection and authored content.
Navigation messages resolve their action from the saved node, never from a frame's
supplied target. Copies remap local targets; removing a target clears its actions.
Desktop captures use a disposable sandboxed renderer with a private
session and disabled page scripts. HTML exports embed styles/assets; the handoff
includes stable targets and comments, plus a selected-artboard PNG on desktop.
Multi-artboard HTML exports use isolated frames to preserve independent viewports
and CSS cascades. Each exported entry includes its reachable screens and keeps a
local playback history, so navigation works offline without an app bridge.

Coding handoff checks the reviewed revision and sends
an immutable snapshot of that proposal, its reachable screens and their comments
to the owning agent. Later design edits cannot change the submitted specification.
Success requires provider acceptance; a rejected request retains the design and
reports the error so the user can review and retry.

Generated Tweaks bind named controls to authored node styles, including CSS
variables. The style remains authoritative; changing or removing a control never
resets its chosen value. Copies receive independent control IDs and targets, and
removing a target removes its controls. Manual CSS outside a control's choices
remains valid and is displayed as a custom value.

Dragging a control previews locally and commits one revision-checked edit on
release. A concurrent edit leaves the preview available for explicit retry or
discard; retry cannot reinterpret a changed control definition. The same
undo history (client-side) and checkpoints (durable) recover both controls and their authored values.

# Backend Protocol

The app-owned JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol between clients (Electron main, companion
clients, SSH peers) and `daemon`, one JSON message per line over stdio, the local
Unix socket and SSH stdio. Provider protocols (Codex app-server, Claude stream
messages, Antigravity ACP, MCP) never cross it.

**The catalog is the code.** Methods are in `core/src/backend-protocol/methods.ts`,
typed params/results in the shared request map, error codes in
`core/src/backend-protocol/rpc.ts`, event unions in `core/src/contracts/events.ts`
(`BackendPublishedEvent`: domain facts, provider conversation frames and explicit
client effects are separate exported unions; `client.connectionChanged` is
renderer-local). This document records the conventions behind them.

## Conventions

Creation commands can return an explicit created-agent identity with their client
snapshot when requested. Callers use that identity rather than inferring a command
outcome from the currently selected agent. Legacy snapshot responses retain their
shape; client navigation remains separate from the shared product operation.

- Names are `resource[/subresource]/verb`, lower camel case, action last.
  Desktop-only and backend-internal renames have no aliases: stale local or remote
  daemons must be restarted or synced. Mobile-consumed contracts follow the
  compatibility rules below, including when routed through shared backend methods.
- State-mutating methods return the authoritative `AppSnapshot`. Mutations persist
  before `snapshot.updated` is published. Read acknowledgments use a bounded agent
  metadata event instead of resending the workspace and complete after persistence.
- Scope prefixes matter: `client/*` methods mutate one client's profile
  (navigation, ordering, preferences) and never another client's; the rest are
  backend-scoped. `_clientId` request metadata selects the profile and is stripped
  before dispatch. Forwarded daemon calls use a separate remote-controller profile,
  never the remote desktop's.
- Client commands never load conversations as a side effect. Clients request
  `agent/conversation/load` explicitly, and snapshot queries perform no
  maintenance (startup maintenance is runtime initialization).
  Conversation loads return the full snapshot and refresh workspace metadata by
  default. Desktop recovery opts into `omitSnapshot: true`: it hydrates provider
  frames without workspace refresh and returns `null`, except that it returns the
  full snapshot when hydration rebinds the agent's backend session, and it is
  rejected while a handoff is in progress. Stdio waits for queued
  output to drain before executing this opt-in so replay frames can be delivered.
  Remote agents retain the full composite snapshot response.
  Clients opt into `reportFailure: true` to receive a safe request error when
  hydration fails, independently of event delivery. Without this flag, failed
  hydration retains its snapshot response and `conversation.historyLoadFailed`
  event for compatibility with released clients.
  Unnegotiated clients retain the default request, response and event semantics.
- Location-scoped methods take optional `remoteConnectionId` / `location`; omitted
  means local. Agent-scoped methods route through the agent's owning location.
- Unsupported optional capabilities answer deterministically: archive returns
  `{ supported: false }`; unsupported history or summary reads are errors, never
  empty successes. Provider catalog UI respects advertised capabilities.
- `driver/*`, `workspace/*` and a few `source/*` methods are backend-internal. Client
  code uses the app-level methods.

## Mobile Compatibility

Mobile applications update independently of the desktop and daemon. Every contract
they consume must remain backwards compatible with shipped clients; desktop-only
contracts are exempt. The boundary includes companion operations, pairing and relay
messages, response framing and encoding, streamed workspace and conversation data,
and the shared or SDK-owned data serialized into those messages. A change in a
producer or dependency is a mobile API change when it changes that wire contract.

- Keep existing method names, accepted request shapes and values, defaults, and
  observable behavior. New request fields must be optional for existing operations.
- Preserve existing response and event fields, their types, nullability, units,
  identifiers and meaning. An additive field or enum/union variant is compatible
  only if shipped decoders can safely consume or ignore it.
- New representations, encodings and behaviors require explicit capability
  negotiation or a separate version while the old path remains available. A
  protocol version bump, app restart or forced mobile update does not preserve
  compatibility. Do not remove legacy handling merely because the current mobile
  source uses the replacement.
- Prove compatibility through the owning runtime with released-client regression
  cases as specified in [testing.md](testing.md#mobile-compatibility-evidence).
  Passing checks against shared current types alone do not establish compatibility.

## Directions

- **Client → daemon:** product requests.
- **daemon → client notifications:** one method, `backend/event/notify`, carrying a
  sequenced `AppBackendEvent` and a small derived `clientState`.
- **daemon → client requests:** host callbacks for native effects only (open
  external, browser open/execute, spoken announcement, permission surfaces),
  currently implemented by Electron. Unknown methods answer `methodNotFound`; a
  throwing callback answers `internalError`. Each side owns the request IDs it
  sends.

## Synchronization

`snapshot/get` returns `{ snapshot, lastEventSeq, clientState }`. The snapshot is
authoritative and transcript-free; between snapshots clients replay only sequenced
`daemon` events through the shared reducer.

Electron and the renderer use a subscribe-buffer-snapshot barrier: subscribe, buffer
notifications while reading `snapshot/get`, discard snapshot-owned events at or below
`lastEventSeq`, apply only contiguous events above it. Provider frames received during or after
a synchronization barrier retain their own revision checks: the product snapshot cannot
replace their transcript data. A gap triggers a fresh
barrier. After a global gap the renderer also invalidates previously cached provider frames
and re-requests conversation snapshots (including inactive and split-pane ones),
because an app snapshot cannot replace a missed provider completion event.
Clients ignore unknown event types.

Provider conversations travel as one bounded reset followed by revisioned deltas in
`codex.conversation*`, `claude.conversation*` and `antigravity.conversation*` frames.
Electron forwards them unreduced; clients validate session identity, reject stale
or gapped revisions and rehydrate through app-owned conversation operations.

Event ingress is untrusted on every transport (stdio, socket, SSH, WebSocket):
decode the complete typed event before publishing. A malformed notification is
logged with structural path/reason only (never payload values) and dropped without
closing the connection or disturbing pending requests. Malformed JSON or JSON-RPC
framing keeps each transport's own error and reconnect policy.

## Lifecycles Owned By The Protocol

- **Agent requests** (approvals, questions, tool confirmations) appear in
  `AppSnapshot.agentRequests` through `agentRequest.created` / `.resolved`, with
  native transcript frames unchanged. Provider handles are never persisted;
  responses route by agent and request ID, guard concurrent submissions, allow retry
  after transport failure, and are invalidated by release or resolution. An
  untargeted response is accepted only when its request ID is unambiguous.
  Codex snapshots reconcile pending client requests, including missed resolutions;
  question lifecycle decisions remain in the provider runtime and are not persisted by Korus.
  Antigravity native questions/approvals use app-owned answered/decision/cancelled
  outcomes; clients never interpret ACP frames.
- **Plan review** persists proposal identity, content and decision status
  (`Agent.planReview`). Replaying a completion never reopens a resolved proposal;
  the response command rejects stale or conflicting decisions, accepts an identical
  one idempotently, and stays pending until prompt acceptance succeeds. Cancel
  submits nothing.
- **Provider authentication:** `provider/authenticate` routes explicit Antigravity
  native login/cancellation to the owning daemon. Connection observations remain
  separate from saved enablement.
- **Provider usage:** quota events update per-engine state; remote quota stays on
  its owning host. Missing utilization is not zero. `provider/usage/get` returning
  `null` means no subscription quota, not a failure. Authentication metadata on
  connection observations is runtime-only and credential-free.
- **Reconnect:** a dropped established connection retries the same transport; it
  never starts a fresh bundled daemon (see
  [backend-architecture.md](backend-architecture.md#transports)).

## Attachments

Local desktop registry resolution is the trusted ingestion boundary; renderer paths
are never provider input. Remote prompts reject them before forwarding until trusted transfer exists.

## Ownership

Product state belongs to `daemon`; Electron and the renderer cache snapshots and
replay events and never invent mutations. Filesystem reads, git, provider tokens
and calls, automations and scheduling stay in `daemon`. Electron owns only native
affordances (windows, menus, dialogs, `openExternal`, native permission callbacks,
speech helper and playback, process launching, transport plumbing).

# Git workflow settings

Status: narrowed scope implemented and validated.
Local commits authorized; no push, merge, publication, release, or automatic review.

## Scope

Settings select how the existing Pull and Update from base operations combine
histories. Preserve their user interaction. Preserve Merge entirely: UI, target
selection, strategies, execution, push, and cleanup.

Settings → Git has two global, immediately autosaved dropdowns:

| Setting | Choices | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pull strategy | Git configuration · Merge · Rebase · Fast-forward only | Git configuration |
| Update from base | Merge · Rebase · Fast-forward only | Merge |

Git configuration is consulted on the owning checkout only when selected. An
unconfigured Pull uses fast-forward only. There is no corresponding Git policy
for updating from a base. No repository overrides, development-state migrations,
one-off strategy dialogs, or additional confirmation steps.

## Execution boundary

- Pull and Update use the saved strategy through the existing backend action.
  Their renderer component and action contracts remain unchanged.
- Preserve target selection, linked-worktree eligibility, dirty-worktree handling,
  progress feedback, and conflict handoff to the agent.
- Rebase conflicts use the same handoff. Instructions tell the agent to inspect
  Git state and continue the native rebase rather than create a merge commit.
  Native Git state survives restart and can be continued or aborted.
- Fast-forward only refuses divergence without fallback. Operations never add
  a push, cleanup, autostash, or an update to unrelated branches.
- No new mutation lock, agent-wide guidance, integration strategies, recovery
  API/banner, remote fetch-all, or branch/head confirmation protocol.

## Implementation and commit checkpoint

One coherent local correction containing production changes and their tests:

1. Restore unrelated changes from the common main baseline.
2. Retain global settings, persistence, normalization, and the Settings UI.
3. Apply strategies only inside Pull and Update from base.
4. Retain the existing conflict workflow with rebase-aware instructions.
5. Validate original merge/action behavior and all configured histories.

## Validation

- Real temporary repositories: merge and rebase histories, fast-forward success
  and refusal, configured Pull, native conflict continuation/abort, dirty changes,
  no unintended pushes/deletions/stashes, and no unrelated-remote dependency.
- App boundary: changing and persisting settings changes the next Update action.
- Mounted UI: settings autosave, errors, choices, original immediate actions,
  and original Merge/Squash interactions.
- Compare complete GitWorkflowControl and merge execution against main.
- Focused tests, full test:ai, lint/typechecks, targeted runtime check, and DoD.
  No release packaging or signing.

## Progress

Unrelated workflow additions restored to the common main baseline. Focused
backend tests (82) and settings/action component tests (54) pass. Full test:ai
passes: 3,796 workspace tests and 47 script tests. All-workspace lint/typechecks,
architecture checks, dead-code checks, and build:web pass.

The complete GitWorkflowControl component, Git operation contracts, and backend
merge implementations match main byte-for-byte. Headless Chromium verified
settings autosave and reload persistence through the owning daemon, including
Update's Fast-forward only choice. It also verified original immediate actions
and Merge/Squash UI using intercepted Git operations. Provider catalog states
were synthetic; no live Git mutations were made by the UI check. Real repository
mutations were exercised by the backend tests. No live SSH or packaged desktop
validation, release packaging, or automatic review.

## Learnings

- A strategy preference changes Git execution, not its surrounding workflow.
  Preserve the action and presentation before adding abstractions.
- Follow existing settings autosave behavior and global scope.
- Use real Git histories to distinguish merge, rebase, and fast-forward behavior.
- Reuse the existing conflict handoff; inspect native Git state when deciding
  how to finish or abort an interrupted update.
