The parent checkout contains unrelated modifications; do not touch them. The sibling SDK is reference/context, not authorization to modify another repository. If an SDK change becomes necessary, explain the concrete boundary and coordinate before expanding scope.

---

**Claude Design: implementation findings and a Korus equivalent**

**Assessment:** Korus can reproduce the useful core of this experience with its existing agent runtimes. The substantial new work is an editable, persistent HTML design surface with safe user/agent changes. A preview pane and a design prompt alone would cover only the first generation.

I inspected the installed **Claude 4.29.0**, extracted its two ASAR archives into a temporary directory, examined the shipped JavaScript and embedded WASM, and inspected the open design through macOS Accessibility and screenshots. I navigated editor controls without changing design content or submitting a prompt. Korus source files were read only; its existing uncommitted changes were preserved.

**What is directly observable**

The current design was open inside a normal conversation, beside the chat. Its canvas offered:

- Pages, artboards, pan/zoom, selection, text, notes, pencil and shapes.
- A layer tree and a Properties panel.
- A Code tab exposing a selected element's CSS and attributes.
- Width/height modes, flex direction, alignment, gap, per-side padding, typography, fill, opacity, radius and borders.
- A Play control for prototype interaction.
- Element/artboard export controls.
- A Tweaks tab whose empty state says Claude can add custom adjustment controls.

The selected layer was a real `div` with CSS such as fixed dimensions, padding, a font stack and flex layout. The artboard content appeared as a nested web document. **For this inspected design, the content is DOM/CSS inside a visual artboard editor.** The UI may also have a separate model for artboard positions and drawing objects; the inspection does not establish every supported document type.

Anthropic publicly describes inline comments, direct edits, generated sliders, imported design systems and handoff/export as parts of the product. Its current product page also describes Design inside conversations. These are product claims, distinct from the local implementation evidence. [Claude Design](https://claude.com/product/design)

**What ships in the desktop app**

| Layer | Evidence | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electron shell | `app.asar` contains `designWindow.js` and Design window creation/navigation code | Native window management is separate from the editor |
| Separate Design window | A sandboxed BrowserWindow calls `loadURL`; Node integration is disabled and context isolation enabled | This path hosts a web experience rather than implementing an editor in native code |
| Native PDF bridge | The Design preload exposes `omeletteDesktopPdf.printFrameToPdf`, with origin checks; main process handles guarded saving | Desktop contributes native export support |
| Bundled web frontend | `ion-dist.asar` includes artifact frame shell, capability broker and replica modules | The installed bundle contains substantial artifact infrastructure |
| Service clients | Design project routes and `anthropic.omelette.api.v1alpha.OmeletteService` clients | There is a hosted service layer; extracting the app is insufficient to reconstruct it |
| Isolated content | Frame code constructs URLs on a separate content host, creates sandboxed iframes and checks message origin/source | Generated content is separated from the trusted application |
| Live document engine | Embedded WASM and JS replica code support DOM/JSON documents, stable IDs, changes, patches, rollback and remote updates | Editing and synchronization are first-class machinery |

The bundle contains both separate Design-window code and the integrated artifact infrastructure seen in the live UI. **Presence of the old window code does not prove the current open artifact uses that path.** Public migration documentation confirms that standalone projects/design systems and integrated artifacts coexist during the transition. [Anthropic migration guide](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17440474-move-from-standalone-claude-design-to-claude)

**The most consequential technical finding**

The shipped `frame-shell-replica` module embeds a Rust/WASM live-document engine. Its binary contains paths such as `api-rs/livedoc/src/v1/dom.rs`, `intent.rs`, `rebase.rs`, `undo.rs` and `patch.rs`. Its exposed operations include:

`openFlatDom`, `openJson`, `applyIntents`, `applyJsonIntents`, `addRemote`, `patchesTo`, `rollback`, `snapshot`, `liveIds`, and `editTowardFlat`.

The surrounding JavaScript handles sequenced changes, author identity, commit conflicts, pulling remote changes and rebasing/retrying certain conflicts. It also pairs DOM subtrees using stable `data-id` attributes.

This is direct evidence of a reusable live document substrate in the artifact host. **It supports the inference that coordinated editing is a major investment, but it does not establish the exact algorithm used by every Design operation.** I did not find sufficient evidence to label it Automerge, Yjs or any particular CRDT.

A reasonable architectural reconstruction is:

```text
Conversation / agent
        │
        ▼
Design operations + current document
        │
        ▼
Persistent, versioned design document
        │
        ├── visual editor and property controls
        ├── isolated DOM/CSS prototype rendering
        ├── comments and targeted change requests
        └── exports / implementation handoff
```

The important product property is that manual edits and agent edits operate on recoverable document state. Regenerating a complete HTML blob after each request makes preserving user changes much harder.

**What remains unknown**

The installed client does not reveal the complete generation prompt, tool schemas, server implementation, design-system retrieval strategy, model routing or screenshot/repair loop. It also does not prove reliable two-way editing of arbitrary React/Vue source.

Anthropic describes codebase/design-file import and component-aware generation. That does not establish that arbitrary production code can round-trip through visual edits without loss. [Design-system setup](https://academy.claude.com/tutorials/create-a-design-system-with-claude)

**How much Korus already has**

| Existing capability | Reuse | Missing piece |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider-backed conversations and app-owned MCP tools | Existing Codex/Claude agents can generate and modify designs | Design-specific document operations and guidance |
| Inline HTML through the conversation SDK | Streaming sandboxed preview, source view and HTML download | Durable design identity, artboards and visual editing |
| In-app browser annotation | Element picking and targeted feedback | Stable design-node identity and revision-aware comments |
| Excalidraw Visualize | Pane UX, selections, annotations and canvas saving patterns | Editable HTML/CSS content |
| Canvas persistence | Expected-revision checks and serialized writes | Equivalent contracts for HTML design operations |

Relevant source:
[canvas document contract](/Users/nbonamy/src/korus-feat-design-workspace/core/src/visualize-canvas.ts:1),
[revision-safe canvas writes](/Users/nbonamy/src/korus-feat-design-workspace/backend/src/visualize-service.ts:271),
[browser element annotations](/Users/nbonamy/src/korus-feat-design-workspace/electron/src/main/browser-pane.ts:309),
[HTML preview in the sibling SDK](/Users/nbonamy/src/codex-app-sdk/packages/vue/src/chat/ChatHtmlBlock.vue:15).

One limit matters: Korus imports Mermaid into editable shapes, but SVG and images are rasterized for Excalidraw. Putting a screenshot of a UI onto that canvas would not make its buttons, text and CSS editable. [Current import behavior](/Users/nbonamy/src/korus-feat-design-workspace/vue/src/components/excalidraw-editor.ts:16)

**Recommended implementation**

Build an app-owned **Design document**, displayed beside the existing conversation. Reuse artifact/pane conventions; give HTML designs their own content model rather than stretching the Excalidraw schema.

For a first version:

1. Persist one or more artboards, an authored HTML node tree with stable IDs, CSS, assets and a revision.
2. Render the design in an isolated frame with an explicit bridge for selection, measurement and preview updates.
3. Offer element comments, text editing and a small style inspector: color, type, padding, gap, size and radius.
4. Route user and agent edits through the same daemon-owned operation service. Require the expected revision; reject stale changes and ask the agent to reread.
5. Keep creation/replacement distinct from subsequent edits. After manual editing begins, use targeted operations and deliberate checkpoints.
6. Support undo and reload persistence; keep Play mode separate from editing.
7. Export self-contained HTML and provide a handoff containing the design, assets, screenshots and intent.

The renderer owns the editor. The daemon owns documents, authorization, persistence and mutations. Electron owns native save/capture effects. Agents use provider-neutral tools such as read design, read selection, apply edits and capture preview; provider transcript ownership remains unchanged.

For editable content, begin with authored HTML/CSS and bounded interactions. Runtime-created nodes and arbitrary framework components need a defined source-mapping strategy before visual edits can reliably reach their source. **Do not promise arbitrary Vue/React round trips in the MVP.**

For design-system fidelity, start with repository tokens, typography, assets and usage guidance. A live component library needs additional bundling, dependency and component-prop contracts. Generated Tweaks can initially be declared controls bound to CSS variables or explicit document properties; the observed tab does not reveal Claude's internal binding API.

**Where the difficult work sits**

- **Edit preservation:** user changes, agent changes, undo and reload must all converge on the same saved state.
- **Source identity:** DOM inspection alone does not reliably identify the authored source of framework-generated content.
- **Layout semantics:** moving a flex/grid child is different from changing an absolutely positioned object's coordinates.
- **Isolation:** an editor bridge must not grant generated scripts access to filesystem, provider credentials or unrestricted app APIs.
- **Output quality:** styling guidance, real assets and visual verification need evaluation against representative designs. The app bundle does not reveal Anthropic's complete quality loop.
- **Exports:** HTML is a practical first target. Editable PowerPoint/Canva output, font fidelity and consistent print layout are separate projects.

**Effort estimate**

These are preliminary engineering ranges, not commitments. They assume one experienced engineer with agent assistance, existing Korus runtimes, a desktop-first local workflow, and a bounded HTML/CSS format. They are cumulative from the start.

| Outcome | Estimated effort | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feasibility spike | 3–5 engineering days | One artboard; selection; one persisted user edit; one revision-safe agent edit; reload proof |
| Useful MVP | 4–6 engineering weeks | Basic artboards, comments, text/style controls, undo/checkpoints, persistence, HTML export and owner-boundary tests |
| Polished local design workspace | 10–16 engineering weeks | Better multi-artboard workflows, layout editing, assets/fonts, design-system support, screenshot tooling, recovery and export polish |
| Broad Claude-like parity | Several engineer-months, likely a small team | Collaborative sharing, rich imports, component integration, advanced controls and multiple high-fidelity export targets |

The spike should test the hardest transition early: **generate a design → manually change text/style → ask the agent to restructure another part → verify manual changes survive → reload → undo/recover.** Add a stale-write case to prove concurrent changes cannot silently overwrite the document.

My recommendation is the bounded local design workspace. It fits Korus's repository context and existing agents, and gives a useful design-to-implementation loop before committing to a general collaborative design platform.

The investigation changed no application code. This report was subsequently saved for the delegated implementation. Tests/builds were unnecessary for the investigation; `git diff --check` passed.

# Automations

Automations send a prompt on a schedule. Use them for a daily project summary, a weekly dependency check, or another task you want an agent to repeat. You can continue an existing conversation or start a fresh Quick Chat for each run.

## Create an automation

1. Open **Automations** from the left rail. Choose **Local** or a connected remote host.
2. Select **New automation** and give it a name.
3. Write the prompt the agent should receive each time.
4. Under **Run in**, choose a team and conversation:
   - **Existing agent** runs in that agent's folder or worktree, with its conversation context.
   - **Existing Quick Chat** continues a chat you already use.
   - **New Quick Chat each run** starts with fresh context. Choose its coding engine, model, and reasoning effort, or leave the model and effort at their defaults.
5. Set the schedule, check **Next run**, and select **Save automation**.

Existing conversations keep the

nversation is busy; it does not interrupt your work or start overlapping runs. Remote automations use the accounts and tools available on the remote computer.

Be explicit about whether the agent may edit files, commit, or publish. Scheduling a prompt does not give it extra permissions.

## Change or stop an automation

Edit the automation to change its prompt, conversation, or schedule. Use the switch in the list to turn it off or on; switching it off stops future runs. This does not stop a run already in progress; interrupt that work from its conversation if needed.

# Conversations

The conversation is where you describe the task, follow the agent's work, and give feedback.

## Send a prompt

Select the agent that owns the task, check its repository folder, and describe the desired outcome in the composer. Include success criteria and constraints:

```text
Add a filter to the issue list. Keep the current sorting, support an
empty result, and check the rendered interaction. Leave the change
uncommitted so I can review it.
```

Use the composer's available context controls to supply file mentions, skills, and attachments. Desktop Antigravity conversations support images, WAV audio, PDFs, and UTF-8 text; its SSH-hosted and browser-hosted conversations do not support attachments. Each agent keeps its own conversation and draft as you switch agents.

Choose a model in the composer before sending when you need a particular provider model. Reasoning effort and speed choices depend on
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
 counters. An interrupted goal can appear paused; a failed run or unverifiable goal state can appear blocked. Clearing a goal removes it rather than claiming it succeeded.

## Resume work

Korus restores durable workspace state when you return. Older messages load through conversation history; use the retry action if history loading reports a failure.

When a provider reports a usage limit with a reset time, the composer shows an **Auto-resume** drawer. Auto-resume is on by default: Korus can continue the conversation when the limit resets. Turn it off in the drawer if you want to resume manually. Pending resumes survive restarts; sending your own prompt or starting a different conversation cancels the pending automatic resume.

Its background daemon can keep agent work running after the desktop window closes. The host still needs to be running and connected; stopping the daemon or sleeping the host interrupts that availability. Check the conversation and current status before submitting another instruction.

# Core concepts

Korus organizes the workspace around agents and the work you give them.

## Teams and agents

A **team** groups agents. An **agent** has an identity, a working folder, provider settings, and its own conversation. Selecting another agent changes the conversation you see while background work can continue.

Use names that communicate responsibility: implementation, documentation, or review, for example. A team groups work; it does not turn the members into one conversation or give them isolated files automatically.

A team can contain agents on this computer and on connected SSH hosts. Each agent's host owns its files and running work. See [Remote hosts](../providers/#remote-hosts) for setup and [Cockpit](../features/workspace#follow-all-teams-in-cockpit) to follow activity across teams.

Use a Quick Chat to discuss an idea without first attaching it to a reposi

me folder still share the same files. A separate conversation does not isolate a checkout.

## Workspace artifacts

The workspace beside the conversation holds documents, plans, files, diffs, and browser previews. Use these surfaces to inspect the work while keeping the discussion available.

Keep the selected agent and artifact context aligned. An agent's status summarizes its activity; the conversation, actual artifact, and validation evidence explain what it accomplished.

## Missions

A Mission is a staged outcome: Requirements, Tickets, Implementation, Review, and Ship. You review the stage artifacts as the work progresses. A Mission is useful when the goal needs shaping and coordinated implementation rather than a single prompt.

## Providers

The provider supplies the coding engine and model access. Korus supplies team coordination, workspace surfaces, and delivery workflows around it. Available controls can differ between engines.

# Your first task

Pick a small outcome so you can learn the workspace while reviewing a manageable diff.

## Check your starting point

1. Connect and enable an engine using its [provider setup guide](../providers/).
2. Open **Existing folder or repository…** and select the checkout you want to work in.
3. Confirm the working folder and branch. Check whether there are already uncommitted changes that must be preserved.
4. Use a dedicated [worktree](../workflows/worktrees) if another agent will write to the same repository or if you want the task isolated.

Korus supplies built-in collaboration and workspace tools to each agent through MCP, without manually adding a server URL or passing an agent ID.

```text
the frontend contract.
```

Name the recipient, what it needs to decide or do, and the information to send. If agents have similar names, include their folder or another distinguishing detail.

# Frequently asked questions

## Does Korus include model access?

Use your connected coding provider's account and plan. Korus supplies the workspace; the provider determines model availability and usage limits.

## Which desktop platforms are supported?

Choose macOS Apple silicon, Windows x64, or Linux x64 / ARM64 from [Downloads](__PRODUCT_DOWNLOAD_URL__). Computer Use and AppShots are macOS-only.

## Do agents share files?

Agents using the same folder share its files. Use separate [worktrees](../workflows/worktrees) for concurrent writers in one repository.

## Does “Separate Korus chats” mean a separate model subscription?

It selects a separate provider setup environment for Korus's chats, sign-in, and configuration. You still use a provider account with the model access you need. Each engine makes this setup choice independently.

See [Provider guides](../providers/) for the exact account, skills, and
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
unknown.

**Clear** removes local statistics, which are retained for up to a year subject to a record limit. It does not stop sharing, remove accepted reports, delete conversations, or change provider quota or billing. Your selected provider still receives the prompts and context needed for its sessions. See the [complete privacy disclosure and field list](__PRODUCT_PRIVACY_URL__#optional-sharing) and [Usage and performance](../features/workspace#understand-usage-and-performance).

## Is a completed task already committed or deployed?

Check the agent's result and Git state. Implementation, validation, commit, push, pull-request creation, merge, and deployment are separate outcomes. Ask explicitly for the delivery action you want.

## When should I use a Mission?

Use a [Mission](../workflows/missions) for an outcome that needs requirements, an implementation breakdown, and explicit stage review. Use an ordinary conversation for a bounded task, or [Code Review](../workflows/code-review) for existing changes.

# Troubleshooting

Start with the action that failed and the error it produced. Preserve unfinished work before changing the setup or restarting a process.

## The app will not launch

Confirm you installed the build matching your platform and architecture. On macOS, move Korus to Applications; Windows builds are unsigned. Record the app version and any error shown during launch. See [Installation](../getting-started/installation) for platform-specific steps.

Development builds have additional runtime and SDK requirements described in the repository README.

## A provider will not connect

1. Open the failing engine's Settings page.
2. Check the selected setup location. A successful login in your normal command-line environment does not authenticate a separate Korus setup.
3. Complete the authentication flow for that selected location. A detected engine and a connected account are separate states.
4. Confirm the engine i
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
d on their own computer. See [Manage agent skills](../providers/#manage-agent-skills).

## Computer Use cannot act

Enable the capability in **Settings → Plugins**, then check **Settings → General → System permissions** for the required macOS access. Record whether discovery, a window observation, an interaction, or capture failed.

## Work stops when the app closes

Check **Settings → General → Keep Korus ready in the background** and its reported daemon status. Distinguish closing the desktop window from intentionally stopping the background service.

When you return, inspect the conversation for an approval, question, or provider error before submitting the same instruction again. Preventing sleep while agents run is a separate General setting.

Include the app version, platform, provider, steps to reproduce, expected result, actual result, and exact error. Use a small reproduction and remove private account details, credentials, and repository content from shared logs or screenshots.

# Code review

Use standalone Code Review when you already have changes to assess in an agent's Git workspace. It supports structured findings, your selection of fixes, and repeated review rounds. A [Mission](./missions#review-and-remediate) has a separate Review stage for its approved feature workflow.

## Before you start

Open the agent working in the checkout you want reviewed. Connect the provider that will do the review, and finish or pause other writers in that folder so the selected change remains stable. An independent reviewer uses the same checkout as the implementation agent; it does not create a worktree.

Choose a working diff, the latest commit, or a branch with changes against its base. Inspect the current folder and branch if the expected diff is missing.

## Start a review

1. Enter `/review` in the agent's composer to open Code Review. Add instructions after the command to focus the review, such as `/

s location. Use it to revisit the findings, your decisions, fixes, and verification results. If the report cannot be saved, the reviewer stays open so you can resolve the error.

Review state is saved while the session is active. If a round fails, read its error, resolve the provider or workspace problem, and use **Retry review** when offered. An existing active review must finish or stop before another starts for the same target. After interrupted work resumes, check the findings and actual files before authorizing more changes.

# Missions

A Mission turns a feature into a staged workflow with an approved brief, repository-owned tickets, implementation evidence, review findings, and delivery tracking.

Use a direct agent conversation for a focused fix or investigation. Use a Mission when you want explicit requirements and ticket approval before implementation, especially when the feature spans repositories. Mission workers are separate Korus agents; they are not simply native subagents of the conversation where you started.

## Prepare the team

Connect the [providers](../providers/) the team will use. Add at least one repository-backed agent to the team before creating a Mission. For a feature spanning an API and a frontend, add an agent for each repository to that same team. Tickets can only target repositories represented in the Mission's team.

Check those repositories have Git history and can create worktrees. Have their setup instru
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
self deliver the Mission.

The Mission completes when every affected repository has a recorded pull request, merge request, or local merge. A created request can still need review and merging. Mission completion does not mean the code was deployed.

## Resume or clean up

Mission stages, accepted artifacts, run status, worktree mappings, and delivery results are saved. Return to the Mission from its team's sidebar to continue. Read a failure's error and fix the underlying setup, provider, or Git issue before retrying. If a stage has no active run or proposal, **Continue mission** can resume it when offered.

To remove a Mission, open its sidebar context menu and choose delete. The confirmation explains that Mission conversations and artifacts will be removed. **Keep worktrees** removes the Mission while preserving its checkouts. **Delete mission and worktrees** also removes the Mission worktrees and local branches and discards uncommitted changes. Preserve anything you still need before choosing that option.

# Parallel agents

Use parallel agents to split an investigation or implementation into work that can be checked independently. Decide who owns each outcome before starting several writers.

## Choose the kind of agent

Korus supports two different forms of delegation:

| Agent | Use it for | Where to follow the work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native subagent | A bounded task inside the current Codex or Claude Code session, such as scanning different parts of a repository. | The parent agent's conversation and the provider's subagent activity. |
| Korus teammate, also called a co-agent | A separately named agent with its own folder and conversation, such as an implementation that needs a dedicated worktree. | Its own entry in the team's sidebar. |

Be explicit in the request. For example:

> Use three native subagents to audit authentication, persistence, and error handling. Keep the scan read-only and consolidate the find
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
tegration owner. For each worktree, inspect the diff, ask for validation evidence, and run [Code Review](./code-review) where useful. Merge in dependency order, then verify the combined behavior. Follow [Worktrees](./worktrees) for merge and cleanup controls.

After reviewing a delegated result, you can ask the agent that created the worker to close it once it is idle. Closing its worker preserves the worktree and branches; it does not merge, delete files, or perform Git cleanup. Request those delivery actions separately when you want them.

If two agents edit the same checkout or overlap unexpectedly, pause one writer, inspect the current diff, and assign ownership before continuing. Preserve the existing changes while resolving the overlap. If a teammate is blocked, send the missing decision or prerequisite to that teammate rather than launching a duplicate implementation.

For a larger feature that needs an approved brief, ticket dependencies, and repository delivery tracking, use a [Mission](./missions).

# Worktrees

A Git worktree gives an agent a separate checkout and branch while keeping it attached to the same repository.

## Before you start

Use a worktree for concurrent implementation, an experiment, or a change you want to keep separate from the current checkout. The folder must belong to a Git repository with a usable base branch. A plain project folder needs Git initialization before it can have worktrees.

A worktree has its own files, index, and checked-out branch. It shares the repository's Git history and remotes. Creating one does not automatically copy uncommitted edits, installed dependencies, ignored environment files, or running services from your original checkout. To move unfinished edits, use [Branch current work](#move-current-work-to-a-new-branch).

Korus's **Worktree initialization** setting controls extra setup. **Auto-detect** uses repository setup instructions when available; othe
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
p them when more work is planned.

The destination checkout must be clean, and the feature branch must include the latest destination commits. If **Merge** reports **Update required**, choose **Update from main** (the label follows your base branch). If the update conflicts, Korus asks the agent to resolve the conflicts in its worktree. Follow the resolution, inspect the diff and checks, then choose **Merge** again. Ask for guidance when a conflict requires a product decision; a branch update does not itself merge into the destination.

When merge cleanup removes the worktree, Korus closes the associated agent after the delivery completes. Retaining the worktree keeps it available for further work. A cleanup warning can mean the merge succeeded while a folder remains; inspect that warning before retrying the merge.

If a push fails after a successful local merge, use **Retry push**. The local merge already exists. Keep a worktree that contains unfinished work, and resolve Git errors before choosing deletion.
